checks.title: A budget with no basis
checks.question: Can every line of the budget be traced to something written down: the estimate range and its assumptions, day rates, environments, licences, running cost and contingency? If the budget runs out in month five, will anyone be able to say which assumption it was built on?
checks.why: The budget was the number the sponsor had left at year end. It matched the low end of the rough estimate, held no running cost and no history load, and was spent before the first report reached production.

evidence.looks_like: A budget broken into people, environments, licences, external services, running cost during the project and contingency, each line pointing to the estimate or a quote, with the estimate's range shown.

signals: The budget is one number with no breakdown.
The budget matches the low end of the estimate range, or the rough estimate from before discovery.
No line for running cost, environments or licences while the project is being built.
checks.contradiction: Compare the budget with the estimate: a budget below the estimate's likely figure, or built from an earlier version of the estimate, is already overspent.
checks.fail_fast: Rebuild the budget from the current estimate's middle figure and put the gap, if any, in front of the sponsor.

checks.title: Spend not tracked against the plan
checks.question: Is actual spend compared with planned spend at least monthly, with a forecast of the total at completion? If the money runs out early, will the status reports from three months before have shown it coming?
checks.why: Contractor invoices went straight to finance. The project manager saw the total only at quarter end, when seventy percent of the budget was gone and forty percent of the work was done.

evidence.looks_like: A monthly table of planned spend, actual spend, forecast to complete and forecast at completion, set against the share of work done, shown in the steering pack.

signals: Status reports mention dates and scope but never money.
Spend is reported as a total so far, with no plan to compare it with and no forecast.
The forecast at completion equals the budget in every report.
checks.contradiction: Compare spend in the status reports with progress against the estimate: money spent faster than work is finished, while the forecast total never changes, means the forecast is not real.
checks.fail_fast: Divide spend so far by the share of work done and compare the answer with the budget today.

checks.title: Nobody owns the running cost after go-live
checks.question: Is the monthly cost of running the solution (compute, storage, licences, support) agreed with the person whose budget will pay it, for this year and next? When the first production bill arrives, whose cost centre is it charged to, and do they know?
checks.why: The project budget ended at go-live. The platform bill landed on the central data team, who had not planned for it, and they switched off the hourly refresh to stay within their own budget.

evidence.looks_like: The running cost figure from the technical estimate, a named budget owner who has accepted it, the cost centre, and a forecast for the next two years that includes data growth.

signals: Running cost is described as "business as usual" or "absorbed by the platform".
The business case shows build cost only.
No named person has agreed to pay the running cost.
checks.contradiction: Compare the running cost estimate in the architecture or discovery document with the business case: a business case without that cost overstates the return.
checks.fail_fast: Send the running cost figure to the person expected to pay it and ask them to confirm it in writing.

checks.title: Bad news held back
checks.question: When the team learns something bad (a slip, a data problem, a design that will not work), how quickly and to whom is it reported, with a next step? Is there anything the team knows today that the sponsor does not?
checks.why: The team knew for six weeks that the source could not deliver hourly data. They hoped to find a workaround and said nothing, so the sponsor learned it from the source owner instead.

evidence.looks_like: Status reports and the issue log that raise problems within days of their discovery, each with an impact and a proposed next step.

signals: Issues appear in the RAID log weeks before they appear in any status report.
Status reports contain only achievements.
Words such as "minor", "under control" or "being looked at" used for issues that later became major.
checks.contradiction: Compare the RAID log dates with status report dates: an issue logged long before it was reported is news that was held back.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the team: "What do we know that we have not told the sponsor?" and report it this week.

checks.title: The current process and reports not written down
checks.question: Is the way the business produces this information today written down: which reports, spreadsheets, extracts and manual steps, who runs them, how often, and who reads them? If an old report keeps being used after go-live, will it be one we never knew existed?
checks.why: The project replaced the monthly sales pack. Nobody had mapped the twelve spreadsheets that fed it, and one of them carried a manual rebate adjustment, so the new numbers were wrong by exactly that amount and the old pack stayed in use.

evidence.looks_like: A current-state inventory: one row per report, spreadsheet or extract being replaced, with its producer, frequency, readers, the sources it pulls from and the manual steps in between.

signals: The discovery document describes the future solution but has no "current state" or "as is" section.
Reports to be replaced are mentioned by name only, with no producer, frequency or readers.
Phrases such as "replaces existing reporting" with no list of what that reporting is.
checks.contradiction: Compare the current-state inventory in the discovery document with the in-scope list: a report or spreadsheet in use today that is neither replaced nor declared out of scope will keep running beside the new system.
checks.fail_fast: Sit for one hour with the person who produces today's main report and write down every step, file and manual change they make.

checks.title: The number the business trusts today not identified
checks.question: For each key figure, which report or person does the business trust today, and has the business agreed that the new system will be judged against it? When the new number differs from the old one, who will decide which is wrong?
checks.why: The new revenue figure was two per cent lower than finance's ledger. Nobody had agreed in advance that the ledger was the reference, so three weeks were lost arguing about whose number was right before anyone looked for the cause.

evidence.looks_like: For each key figure, the trusted reference (report, ledger, application screen), who owns it, a sample value for a known period, and whether the business believes that reference is itself correct.

signals: No reference report or trusted figure is named anywhere in the requirements or test strategy.
The requirements say the new figures must be "accurate" or "correct" without saying compared with what.
The trusted figure is named but nobody has captured a value for a known period.
checks.contradiction: Compare the requirements with the test strategy: if the requirements name a trusted report but the reconciliation tests compare against something else, or nothing, acceptance will be argued, not tested.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the business owner for last month's value of the top three figures and where they got it, and store the screenshots with the requirements.

checks.title: Decisions the data will drive not named
checks.question: Which decisions will people make with this data, how often, and what do they do today instead? If the project delivers every table and report on time but nothing changes in the business, will it be because nobody said which decision it was for?
checks.why: The team built a full customer model because "the business needs a single view of the customer". The one decision it was actually needed for, which customers to call each Monday, required a field that was never captured.

evidence.looks_like: A short list of decisions, each with who makes it, how often, what information they need to make it, what they use today, and what is painful about that.

signals: Requirements list data and reports but never the decision or action they support.
The problem statement is about technology ("legacy reporting", "move to the cloud") rather than a business pain.
Words such as "insight", "visibility" or "single view" appear without a named decision.
checks.contradiction: Compare the decisions in the discovery document with the freshness and grain in the requirements: a daily decision served by monthly data, or a decision about individual customers served by totals, means the two were not connected.
checks.fail_fast: Ask three intended users: "What will you do differently on the day this is live?" and write the answers against the requirements.

checks.title: Manual adjustments hidden in today's numbers
checks.question: Do today's trusted figures include manual adjustments, hand-kept mappings, overrides or exclusions that live in someone's spreadsheet or head, and has each one been listed with a decision to automate it, keep it manual, or drop it? If the new numbers never match the old ones, will it be because of a correction nobody told us about?
checks.why: Each month an analyst removed two intercompany customers and reclassified a product line by hand before the board pack went out. The new system did neither, and it took a month of reconciliation to find out why.

evidence.looks_like: A list of every manual adjustment, override, exclusion and hand-kept mapping in today's process, with its size, who makes it, why, and whether the new system will automate it, keep it as a governed manual input, or stop it.

signals: The current state is described as "extracted from the source system" with no manual steps.
Spreadsheets are mentioned as inputs to today's report with no description of what they change.
No requirement covers manual inputs, overrides or exclusions.
checks.contradiction: Compare the current-state description with the business rules or data model: an adjustment people make today that has no rule, no manual input and no "dropped" decision will show up as an unexplained difference.
checks.fail_fast: Take last month's trusted figure and the raw source total for the same period; ask the report owner to explain the difference line by line.

checks.title: Sources not named, each with an owner
checks.question: Is every source the requirements depend on named, with the system, the data needed from it, and a named person who owns it and can answer questions about it? If a source turns out to be unavailable in the build, will we find out then, or now?
checks.why: The requirements said "customer and order data". In the build the team learned that returns lived in a separate warehouse system nobody had listed, owned by a team that had no time for the project that quarter.

evidence.looks_like: A source list: one row per source with the system, the business data it provides, the requirements that need it, the source owner's name, and whether access has been requested.

signals: Data needs are described as subjects ("customer data", "sales data") with no system named.
Sources are listed without an owner, or with a team name instead of a person.
A source appears in the architecture that is not in the requirements, or the reverse.
checks.contradiction: Compare the source list in the requirements with the sources drawn in the architecture: a source in one and not the other is either unneeded work or a missing dependency.
checks.fail_fast: For each requirement, write the source system it comes from; any requirement you cannot fill in is a gap to raise this week.

checks.title: Grain the users need not compared with the grain the sources hold
checks.question: For each requirement, what level of detail do the users need (each transaction, each customer per day, each store per month), and does the source hold data at that level? If users ask to drill into a total after go-live, will the detail exist?
checks.why: Users needed sales by individual product. The source only kept daily totals by product group, which nobody checked until the first drill-down in user testing.

evidence.looks_like: For each key requirement, the grain needed in plain words (for example "one row per order line per day"), the grain available at the source, and how any gap was resolved.

signals: Requirements say "by product", "by customer" or "detail" without saying the lowest level needed.
Drill-down or "detail" is requested with no statement of how far down.
The data model's grain is finer or coarser than anything stated in the requirements.
checks.contradiction: Compare the grain in the requirements with the grain of the tables in the data model: a requirement needing more detail than its table holds cannot be met.
checks.fail_fast: Show users one real row from the source and ask: "Is this the smallest thing you will ever need to see?"

checks.title: Freshness not tied to a decision
checks.question: How fresh must the data be, as a time of day or a delay in minutes or hours, and which decision or action needs it that fresh? If the business later asks for faster data, will we know whether the decision really needs it?
checks.why: The sponsor asked for hourly data. The only decision it served was a weekly stock order, so the team built and paid for hourly loads that nobody looked at between Mondays.

evidence.looks_like: For each consumer or report, a freshness target such as "ready by 7 a.m. local time on working days" or "within fifteen minutes of the sale", paired with the decision that needs it and what happens if it is late.

signals: Freshness is stated as "real-time", "up to date" or "latest" with no number.
One freshness target is stated for everything, with no difference between consumers.
No reason or decision is given for the freshness asked for.
checks.contradiction: Compare the freshness in the requirements with the decisions in the discovery document: data needed faster than the decision it serves is cost with no benefit, and slower is a decision made on stale data.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the user: "If this arrived at noon instead of 7 a.m., what would you do differently?" and price the two options side by side.

checks.title: No business rule for late and corrected data
checks.question: When data arrives late or a past figure is corrected, what should the business see: should last month change, which date decides the period (order, shipment, invoice or posting date), and when is a period closed and never restated? If a published figure changes after the board has seen it, has the business agreed that it may?
checks.why: Returns posted in March for February sales changed February's revenue after it had gone to the board. The finance director had assumed closed months never change, the team had assumed they always do, and neither was written down.

evidence.looks_like: A short restatement policy: which date assigns a record to a period, how far back corrections may change published figures, when a period closes, and how users are told that a past figure changed.

signals: The requirements never mention late data, corrections, restatement, closing or period end.
The date that decides the reporting period is not stated for any measure.
Late and corrected data is marked as a technical matter only.
checks.contradiction: Compare the restatement policy in the requirements with the late-data handling in the architecture: if the architecture rebuilds past periods but the business expects closed periods to be frozen, or the reverse, one of them is wrong.
checks.fail_fast: Show the business owner one real correction from last month and ask which month it should change and whether anyone must be told.

checks.title: No source of truth when systems disagree
checks.question: When two sources hold the same thing differently (a customer's address in the sales system and the billing system, a product's price in two catalogues), which one wins, for which fields, and who decided? When a user finds the two disagree after go-live, which written decision answers them?
checks.why: The sales and billing systems had different customer segments. The team picked one, the business assumed the other, and every segment report was disputed until the decision was made at steering level.

evidence.looks_like: For each shared business entity, a recorded decision on which source wins for which fields, what happens when a record exists in only one, and who owns the decision.

signals: The same entity (customer, product, employee, site) comes from more than one source with no rule for which wins.
Phrases such as "merge customer data" or "single customer view" with no matching rule.
The decision log has no entry about sources of truth.
checks.contradiction: Compare the source list with the decision log: every entity supplied by two or more sources needs a decision recorded; any without one will be decided silently in code.
checks.fail_fast: Pull twenty customers that exist in both systems, show the differences to the business owner, and ask which column wins for each field.

checks.title: Job retries, concurrency and repair are safe
checks.question: Are task retries, timeouts, maximum concurrent runs and queueing set deliberately for each job, and is every task safe to rerun from the start, as a repair run does?
checks.why: Operations repaired a failed run; the failed task had appended half its rows before failing, and the repair appended them again.

evidence.looks_like: Retry and timeout settings per task in the bundle, concurrency left at one, and a runbook note on repair.

checks.fail_fast: Cancel a task halfway in test, repair the run, and compare the output with a clean run.

checks.title: AUTO CDC sequenced by a real source order
checks.question: Where AUTO CDC builds SCD tables, is SEQUENCE BY a column that truly reflects source change order (with a tie-breaker), not the time the row landed?
checks.why: Sequencing used the file arrival time; a delayed file replayed older updates as newest, and SCD type 2 history showed customers moving back to old addresses.

evidence.looks_like: The sequence column per source, how ties are broken (STRUCT of columns), and the delete condition.

checks.fail_fast: Ask the source owner which column orders changes, and check for ties in a real change extract.

checks.title: Detecting hard deletes at the source
checks.question: When a record is physically deleted in the source, how does the platform find out?
checks.why: Cancelled orders were deleted in the source, but the incremental extract only picked up new and changed rows, so the cancelled orders stayed in the warehouse and inflated sales.

evidence.looks_like: For each source, whether deletes happen and how they are captured: change capture with delete events, a periodic full key comparison, or a delete feed from the source.

signals: Incremental loads use a modified-date filter and deletes are not mentioned.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the source owner whether rows are ever deleted, then delete a test row in a source test system and run the load; the platform must reflect it.

databricks.do: With CDC feeds use AUTO CDC ... APPLY AS DELETE WHEN, or MERGE ... WHEN MATCHED AND op = 'D' THEN DELETE; without CDC, compare full key snapshots (AUTO CDC FROM SNAPSHOT treats missing keys as deleted) or use MERGE ... WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE.
databricks.verify: Delete a row in a source test system and check it disappears or is flagged after the load.
databricks.traps: WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE against a partial extract deletes everything not in that extract.

checks.title: A thin slice proved the design end to end
checks.question: Has one source table been pushed through every layer to one report or query in a production-like environment, before the design was signed off?
checks.why: A clean architecture diagram was signed off without ever running; in MVP 1 the team found the source format, network and permissions all differed from the assumptions.

evidence.looks_like: A description of the thin slice, where it ran, what it proved, what it found, and how the design changed as a result.

signals: The architecture shows only target-state diagrams with no evidence of anything having run.
checks.fail_fast: Choose the riskiest source and the most important report, and connect them with the simplest possible pipeline this week.

checks.title: Non-functional needs written as numbers
checks.question: Are the non-functional needs (freshness, volume, recovery, availability, retention, concurrency) written as measurable numbers and agreed with the business?
checks.why: "Near real time" meant five seconds to the business and an hour to the engineers; the gap was found at user acceptance and the design had to be rebuilt.

evidence.looks_like: A table of non-functional needs, each with a number, a measurement method and who agreed it.

signals: Words like "fast", "near real time", "scalable" or "highly available" with no numbers.
checks.fail_fast: Rewrite each non-functional sentence as a number and ask the business owner to confirm it.

checks.title: Grain and keys of every table
checks.question: Is the grain (what one row means) and the key of every target table written down and agreed?
checks.why: The orders table mixed order headers and order lines; summing it double-counted shipping, and two teams built different fixes.

evidence.looks_like: For each table: one sentence for the grain, the key columns, and a uniqueness test on that key.

checks.fail_fast: For each target table, finish the sentence "one row is one …" and test the key for uniqueness.

checks.title: Data quality rules written with owners
checks.question: Which data quality rules apply to each important table, who owns each rule, and are they written down as checks that run on every load?
checks.why: Everyone assumed someone else checked that order totals were positive; a source bug sent negative totals for a week and nobody's check caught it.

evidence.looks_like: A rule list per table (not null, unique, valid values, ranges, referential integrity, business rules), each with a business owner and a severity, implemented as automated checks.

signals: The documents say "data quality checks will be applied" with no list of rules.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the business owner for the five things that would make them distrust the main report, and write each as a rule that runs on today's data.

databricks.do: In Lakeflow pipelines write rules as expectations (EXPECT ... ON VIOLATION DROP ROW / FAIL UPDATE); elsewhere use CHECK and NOT NULL constraints plus a test framework in jobs.
databricks.verify: Query the pipeline event log or Data quality tab for pass and fail counts per rule.

checks.title: What happens to a row that fails a rule
checks.question: When a row fails a rule, is the batch rejected, the row quarantined, or the row loaded and flagged, and who is told and fixes it?
checks.why: Bad rows were filtered out silently; three thousand orders a day disappeared into a table no one looked at, and sales were understated for a quarter.

evidence.looks_like: An action per rule severity, a quarantine table with reasons, a count of quarantined rows reported to an owner, and a way to reprocess rows once fixed.

checks.fail_fast: Feed a sample with known bad rows in test and check each lands where the design says, with a reason, and that an owner is notified.

databricks.do: Use warn or drop expectations, and write failing rows to a quarantine table with an inverted expectation so they are kept with a reason, not just counted.
databricks.verify: Load known-bad rows in test and find each one in quarantine.
databricks.traps: expect_or_drop only counts dropped rows; the rows themselves are gone unless you quarantine them.

checks.title: A source goes quiet or sends far too little
checks.question: Does anything detect a source that sends no data, an empty file, or a much smaller or larger volume than usual?
checks.why: The source sent an empty file after a failed export; the load succeeded, every job was green, and the business saw a day with zero sales before any engineer did.

evidence.looks_like: Freshness and volume checks per source with expected ranges, which fail or alert rather than load quietly.

signals: Monitoring is described only as "job failure alerts".
checks.fail_fast: Run a load with an empty input in test; it must not complete as a green success without someone being told.

databricks.do: Enable data quality monitoring on the schema for freshness and completeness, and add a row-count check task that fails on empty or abnormal batches; alert with Databricks SQL alerts.
databricks.verify: Load an empty file in test and confirm an alert fires.
databricks.traps: Monitoring results arrive after the load; a gate inside the job is still needed to stop bad data reaching gold.

checks.title: Real data profiled before design
checks.question: Has real data from every source been profiled (nulls, duplicates, broken keys, odd values, volumes), and was the profile shown to the business owner?
checks.why: The design assumed every order had a customer; profiling in build week three found twenty percent did not, and the model and estimate both had to be redone.

evidence.looks_like: A profile per source table from a real extract (not a sample built by hand), with findings and what was decided about each.

signals: Discovery describes sources from documentation only, with no profiling results.
checks.fail_fast: Pull a real extract of the biggest source table this week and count nulls, duplicates and orphan keys in the columns the design relies on.

databricks.do: Profile real extracts with SQL in a notebook or with data profiling on the bronze tables.

checks.title: Same batch or file arriving twice
checks.question: How is a file, batch or extract that arrives a second time prevented from doubling the numbers?
checks.why: After an outage the source resent yesterday's file, the pipeline loaded it again as new, and revenue on the dashboard doubled for a day before anyone noticed.

evidence.looks_like: A business key or file fingerprint, a record of what has already been loaded, and a test that loads the same input twice.

signals: The architecture describes loads as appends with no key, fingerprint or load register.
The test strategy has no test that resends an input.
checks.fail_fast: Load the same file twice in a test environment; row counts and key totals in every layer must not change after the second load.

databricks.do: Ingest files with Auto Loader or COPY INTO, which both remember files already loaded. Write to silver with MERGE on the business key, not append.
databricks.verify: Re-drop the same file and rerun; DESCRIBE HISTORY on the target shows no rows inserted (operationMetrics numTargetRowsInserted = 0).
databricks.traps: A file renamed or rewritten by the source counts as new to Auto Loader. Its checkpoint is the memory: deleting or moving it reloads everything.

checks.title: Rerunning a job changes the result
checks.question: If a job is run again for the same period, does it produce exactly the same result (is every step idempotent)?
checks.why: Operations reran a failed nightly job, but its first half had already appended rows, so the fact table held two copies of the night's orders until month-end reconciliation found them.

evidence.looks_like: Each write described as merge on a key, or replace of a whole partition or period, never a blind append; a rerun test per pipeline; the runbook says reruns are safe.

signals: Writes are described as "insert" or "append" with no key or partition overwrite.
The runbook warns operators not to rerun, or says to clean up by hand before rerunning.
checks.fail_fast: Run the pipeline twice in a row for the same day in test and compare a fingerprint of every output table (counts, sums of key measures); they must be identical.

databricks.do: Use MERGE on a key, or INSERT OVERWRITE / replaceWhere for a whole date range, for every write a rerun could repeat.
databricks.verify: Run the job twice for the same period; compare counts and DESCRIBE HISTORY metrics between runs.
databricks.traps: Repairing a failed Lakeflow Jobs run reruns failed tasks from the start; a task that appended before failing will append again.

checks.title: Duplicates already inside the source
checks.question: Does each source have a reliable unique key, and what is the rule when the source itself sends two rows for the same thing?
checks.why: The source table had no primary key and sent the same customer twice with different spellings; joins to it multiplied order rows and inflated sales by eight percent.

evidence.looks_like: A profile showing key uniqueness per source table, the chosen business key, and an agreed rule for duplicates (keep latest, keep all, reject), signed by the data owner.

signals: The data model lists tables without a key, or says "key to be confirmed".
No profiling results for key uniqueness are recorded.
checks.fail_fast: Count rows per proposed key in a real extract of every source table; any key with more than one row needs a written rule before design continues.

databricks.do: Profile key uniqueness with a GROUP BY key HAVING count(*) > 1 query; deduplicate in silver with a window (row_number over key ordered by a change timestamp) before MERGE.
databricks.verify: A uniqueness expectation or test on the silver key runs on every load.
databricks.traps: MERGE fails when several source rows match one target row; deduplicate the source batch first. PRIMARY KEY constraints in Unity Catalog are informational and are not enforced.

checks.title: Replayed events in a stream
checks.question: When the stream redelivers events after a restart or failure (at-least-once delivery), how does the target avoid counting them twice?
checks.why: A consumer restarted from an older position and replayed two hours of events; the counts sink appended them again and the real-time dashboard overstated traffic for the day.

evidence.looks_like: An event id or key plus sequence used to deduplicate, a stated delivery guarantee end to end, and an idempotent or transactional write to the sink.

signals: The design assumes "exactly once" without saying which component provides it.
checks.fail_fast: In test, stop the stream mid-flow, rewind its position by a known number of events, restart, and confirm output counts match the input exactly.

databricks.do: In Structured Streaming use dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark on an event id, and idempotent writes in foreachBatch (MERGE, or txnAppId plus txnVersion options).
databricks.verify: Restart a stream from an older checkpoint copy in test and compare counts.
databricks.traps: dropDuplicates without a watermark keeps state forever and grows until the job slows or fails.

checks.title: Access through groups and service identities
checks.question: Is access granted to groups by role with least privilege, and do scheduled jobs run as service identities rather than as a person?
checks.why: Production jobs ran under the lead developer's own account; when she left the company her account was disabled and every nightly job failed.

evidence.looks_like: A role-to-group access model, service identities for jobs in each environment, no direct user grants in production, and who approves access requests.

checks.fail_fast: List who owns and runs each production job; any job owned or run by a named person is a gap.

databricks.do: Grant privileges to account groups, make groups (not people) owners of catalogs, schemas and jobs, and run jobs as service principals.
databricks.verify: Check job run_as and object owners; none should be a named person in production.

checks.title: Network path to every source proven early
checks.question: Has a connection from the platform to every source and target been made in a real environment, through firewalls, private links and credentials?
checks.why: The source sat in a data centre behind a firewall; the network change took nine weeks of tickets and MVP 1 waited for it with the team idle.

evidence.looks_like: Each source and target with its connection method, the network changes required, their lead time, and evidence a test connection succeeded.

signals: Connectivity appears as an assumption in the risk log with no date.
checks.fail_fast: Raise the network and credential requests in week one of discovery and pull one row from every source.

databricks.do: For private sources, plan private connectivity (for serverless, network connectivity configurations) and Unity Catalog connections or credentials early.
databricks.traps: Serverless and classic compute reach the network differently; prove the route for the compute you will really use.

checks.title: The rough guess became the promise
checks.question: Has the estimate been redone since the first rough guess, and does everyone quoting a date or a budget know which version they are quoting? Imagine it is six months from now and the project is late: was the date we are judged against the one somebody guessed before anyone looked at the data?
checks.why: A number given in a corridor before discovery was written into the budget. Discovery found twice the work, but the plan was expected to confirm the guess, so the project was "late" from its first week.

evidence.looks_like: An estimate history showing the rough estimate, the discovery estimate and later re-estimates, each dated, with the baseline that sign-off accepted clearly marked.

signals: The same number appears in the first brief, the discovery document and the plan, unchanged.
The estimate has no date or version, so nobody can tell whether it came before or after discovery.
Status reports measure progress against a figure that is older than the discovery document.
Phrases such as "as agreed at the outset" or "the approved budget" with no link to how it was built.
checks.contradiction: Compare the estimate with the plan: if the plan's end date or budget matches the stage-2 rough estimate rather than the discovery estimate, the guess has become the promise.
checks.fail_fast: Put the rough estimate and the discovery estimate side by side in front of the sponsor and ask which one the plan is built on.

checks.title: One number instead of a range
checks.question: Is the estimate given as a range, with the reason for its width? If the project overruns, will anyone be able to say whether the overrun was inside the range we said was possible?
checks.why: "Six weeks" was heard as a commitment. "Five to eight weeks if access arrives in week one" would have been a plan, and the slip to seven weeks would have been expected rather than a crisis.

evidence.looks_like: A low and a high figure (or a most-likely figure with a stated spread), and a sentence on what would move it toward either end.

signals: The estimate is a single figure in days, weeks or money with no low and high value.
The width of the range does not narrow from the rough estimate to the discovery estimate.
The range is the same percentage on every item, which suggests it was added, not reasoned.
checks.contradiction: Compare the estimate with the status reports: a range in the estimate but a single committed date in every status report means the range was dropped on the way to the stakeholders.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the person who wrote the estimate for the worst realistic case. If they can name one without hesitating, it belongs in the document.

checks.title: An estimate with no written assumptions
checks.question: Which assumptions does the estimate depend on, and which one, if wrong, would move it the most? If the estimate turns out wrong, will we be able to point to the assumption that broke?
checks.why: The estimate assumed the source data was clean and that one person would test. Neither was written down, so when both failed, the overrun looked like the team's fault instead of a known risk.

evidence.looks_like: A numbered list of assumptions next to the estimate, the most sensitive ones marked, and each one also logged in the RAID log with an owner.

signals: No "assumptions" heading or list anywhere in or near the estimate.
Assumptions are written as one line, such as "standard assumptions apply".
Assumptions exist in the estimate but none of them appear in the RAID log.
checks.contradiction: Compare the estimate's assumptions with the RAID log: an assumption in one but not the other is either unmanaged or was never the real basis of the estimate.
checks.fail_fast: Pick the riskiest assumption and test it this week, for example by requesting the access or pulling one real extract.

checks.title: Invisible work left out of the estimate
checks.question: Does the estimate include the work that is not building: getting access, setting up environments, testing, fixing data, rehearsing the cut-over, documentation and handover? If we run out of time, will it be because the build took longer, or because this work was never counted?
checks.why: The build finished on time. Then access approvals, test data, two cut-over rehearsals and the runbook took another five weeks that nobody had planned for.

evidence.looks_like: Separate lines for access and onboarding, environments, testing (including reconciliation and user acceptance), data fixes, history load, cut-over and rollback rehearsal, runbook, handover and hypercare.

signals: The estimate lists only build items (pipelines, tables, reports).
Testing is a fixed percentage added at the end rather than counted per item.
Words such as "cut-over", "handover", "access", "environment" or "hypercare" do not appear in the estimate.
checks.contradiction: Compare the estimate with the plan: plan tasks for testing, cut-over or handover that have no matching line in the estimate are unfunded work.
checks.fail_fast: Read the estimate against the ten lifecycle stages and ask, for each stage after build, which line pays for it.

checks.title: Never corrected against actual progress
checks.question: Is actual effort compared with the estimate at least every two weeks, and has the estimate been changed when the real rate differed? If we finish late, will we have known it two months before or two days before?
checks.why: The thin slice took three times longer than planned per table. Nobody re-estimated, and the gap only showed when the last month of the plan arrived with half the tables still to build.

evidence.looks_like: A re-estimate after the thin slice and then every two weeks, showing items done, the real rate, and the forecast finish, with changes explained.

signals: The estimate document has one version and its date is before build started.
Status reports show percent complete but never a forecast end date or rate.
No mention of a thin slice or of the rate it achieved.
checks.contradiction: Compare status reports with the estimate: if progress reports show fewer items finished than the estimate's rate predicts, but the end date never moves, the estimate is not being corrected.
checks.fail_fast: Divide items finished so far by weeks spent, and project the finish date from that rate today.

checks.title: History load and data fixing underestimated
checks.question: Has the work of loading history and dealing with poor source data been estimated separately, using a profile of the real data? If the history load is what delays go-live, will that surprise anyone?
checks.why: The pipelines worked on a month of data. Ten years of history held old codes, broken keys and a format change, and checking the old numbers with the business took longer than building the pipelines.

evidence.looks_like: Separate estimate lines for the history load (volume, number of runs, reconciliation with the business) and for data fixes, sized from a profile of real data.

signals: The history load is not mentioned in the estimate, or it is one line with a small number.
The estimate says data quality is "assumed acceptable" with no profile behind it.
There is no data profiling section in the discovery document.
checks.contradiction: Compare the discovery profiling results with the estimate: if the profile found quality problems but the estimate has no line for fixing or handling them, the estimate ignored the evidence.
checks.fail_fast: Load one year of real history in a test environment and time it, and count the rows that fail basic rules.

checks.title: A steering group that cannot decide
checks.question: Does the steering group include people who can decide on money, scope and dates, plus the owners of the data and the platform the project depends on, and is it written down what it decides and how often it meets? When the project needs a yes on extra budget or a later date, will the people in the room be able to give it?
checks.why: The steering group was the project team's managers. When the source team refused to change their extract, nobody in the room had authority over them, and the issue went round the meeting for two months.

evidence.looks_like: Short terms of reference: members by name, what the group decides (budget, scope, dates, go-live), how often it meets, and attendance records showing the deciders actually came.

signals: No steering group or terms of reference is written down.
Members are all from the delivery side, with no data owner, source owner or budget holder.
Steering notes record updates but no decisions.
checks.contradiction: Compare the steering membership with the RAID log's biggest dependencies and issues: an issue owned by a team nobody on the steering group can direct will not be solved there.
checks.fail_fast: Take the top open issue to the next steering meeting and see whether anyone there can decide it.

checks.title: Stage gates with no exit criteria
checks.question: Do discovery sign-off, production sign-off and project sign-off each have written exit criteria and the evidence each needs (for example reconciled numbers, clean runs, an accepted support model, measured benefits), agreed before the gate? At each gate, are we deciding on evidence or on the calendar?
checks.why: Production sign-off was a meeting on the planned date. It was signed with reconciliation still failing for two regions, and the project team was released, so the differences were never explained.

evidence.looks_like: For each gate, a short list of exit criteria with the document or test result that proves each one, who signs, and the possible outcomes (go, go with conditions, stop).

signals: Gates appear in the plan as dates only.
Production or project sign-off has no criteria, or criteria such as "all work complete".
Sign-off records do not mention which criteria were met.
checks.contradiction: Compare each gate's sign-off record with its exit criteria and the evidence available on that date: a gate signed while a criterion was unmet was passed on the date, not the evidence.
checks.fail_fast: Write the production sign-off criteria now and check which of them the project could meet today.

checks.title: Approval boards and their calendars not on the plan
checks.question: Are the outside approvals the project needs (architecture review, security review, privacy assessment, data sharing agreement, change board) listed with their meeting dates, what they need submitted and how long they take? Which board meets monthly and has not yet heard of us?
checks.why: The privacy assessment had to be approved before personal data could be copied to the new platform. The board met monthly, sent the first submission back, and the project lost two months it had not planned for.

evidence.looks_like: A list of approvals with the board, its meeting calendar, the submission deadline, what it needs, the usual number of rounds, and the plan tasks that wait on it.

signals: No approvals or review boards appear in the plan.
Personal or sensitive data is in scope but no privacy assessment or data sharing agreement is mentioned.
Approvals are planned in the same week the work that needs them starts.
checks.contradiction: Compare the architecture's personal data flows and platform changes with the plan's approvals: each one that needs a board's approval, with no slot booked, is an unplanned wait.
checks.fail_fast: Ask security and the architecture board which approvals this project needs and the next date each one meets.

checks.title: Runbook missing or written at the end
checks.question: Is there a runbook that operations have read and used: what runs when, how to tell it failed, how to rerun safely, and who to call? If a load fails on the first night after the team has gone, can operations fix it?
checks.why: The runbook was written in the last week and never tried. On the first failure operations reran the whole load, which doubled a month of figures.

evidence.looks_like: A runbook started in build and finished before deploy, covering schedule, monitoring, alerts, common failures with fixes, safe rerun steps and contacts, used in at least one failure drill.

signals: No runbook or operations guide among the documents.
The runbook is planned only for the last week before go-live.
The runbook has headings but sections marked "to be completed".
checks.contradiction: Compare the runbook with the architecture: jobs, sources or failure points in the architecture that the runbook does not mention will be unsupported.
checks.fail_fast: Break one job in the test environment and ask operations to recover it using only the runbook.

checks.title: Knowledge transfer never tested
checks.question: Has the support team made at least one real change and one real recovery while the project team watched? If the project team left tomorrow, could the support team run and change this system?
checks.why: Knowledge transfer was two presentation sessions. The first change request after closure took the support team a month, and the project team had to be called back.

evidence.looks_like: Planned handover sessions with hands-on tasks, and a record of a change and a recovery done by the support team themselves.

signals: Knowledge transfer is a single line or a few presentation sessions in the plan.
The support team is not named, or joins only at the end.
No hands-on tasks are planned for the support team.
checks.contradiction: Compare the plan's handover time with the size of the system in the architecture: a short handover for a large system means much will not transfer.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the support team to make one small real change this sprint, with the project team only watching.

checks.title: Support model not agreed
checks.question: Is it agreed who supports the system after go-live, in which hours, how fast they respond, how long the project team stays during the early weeks, and who pays? On the first weekend in production, who answers a failure?
checks.why: The project assumed the central support team would take over; the support team assumed the project would. After go-live a failed weekend load went unnoticed until Monday morning.

evidence.looks_like: A signed support model: support team, hours, response times, escalation, early-life support period, and the criteria for ending it.

signals: No support model, or one that says "business as usual support".
The support team has not been asked to accept the system.
Support hours do not match the freshness promised to users.
checks.contradiction: Compare the support model with the non-functional requirements: data promised by 7 a.m. but support starting at 9 a.m. means nobody fixes a night failure in time.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the support team lead whether they have agreed to take this system, and on what terms.

checks.title: History load scope and approach
checks.question: How much history will be loaded, from where, and by what approach (one go, in phases, or from archive), and who checks the old numbers?
checks.why: The plan assumed history would come from the same feed as daily loads, but the source only kept ninety days; five years had to come from an archive in another format, adding six weeks.

evidence.looks_like: The number of years in scope, where each year comes from, the load approach and order, the expected volume, and who signs off that historical numbers are right.

signals: History is not mentioned, or "history to be loaded" appears with no years or source.
The plan has no task or time for the history load.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the source owner how far back the source really holds data, and pull one month of the oldest year in scope through the pipeline.

databricks.do: Load history into the same bronze tables as daily loads, by date chunk, from archive files or a source extract; record the chunks in a control table.
databricks.verify: Reconcile each historical year against the source or finance before switching on daily loads.

checks.title: Handing over from history load to incremental loads
checks.question: How does the switch from the history or full load to incremental loads avoid both a gap and an overlap in the data?
checks.why: The full snapshot finished at 10:00 but incremental capture was started at 11:00; an hour of changes was never loaded and the totals were quietly short for months.

evidence.looks_like: A defined high-water mark or change position taken before the snapshot starts, incremental capture starting from it, and overlapping rows absorbed by a merge on key.

checks.fail_fast: In test, change rows in the source while the full load runs, then start incremental; every changed row must appear once with its latest value.

databricks.do: With Lakeflow pipelines, AUTO CDC with SEQUENCE BY absorbs overlap between the snapshot and the change feed; otherwise MERGE with a sequence column so older changes never overwrite newer.
databricks.verify: Change rows during the snapshot in test and check each ends with its latest value once.

checks.title: Late and corrected rows rebuild the right periods
checks.question: When rows arrive late or yesterday's figures are corrected next week, which periods are rebuilt, and how far back can corrections reach?
checks.why: Returns were booked against sales from three weeks earlier, but the pipeline only rebuilt the last two days, so monthly net revenue never matched the finance ledger.

evidence.looks_like: A profile of how late data really arrives, an agreed correction window, and a design that reprocesses affected periods by business date rather than load date.

signals: Aggregates are described as built "for the load date" only.
Nothing in the discovery document says how late source data can arrive.
checks.fail_fast: In a real extract, compare business date against load date and find the longest lag; then insert a row two weeks late in test and check the monthly total updates.

databricks.do: Rebuild aggregates for affected business dates with MERGE or replaceWhere driven by the dates present in the incoming batch; Change Data Feed on silver can tell gold which keys changed.
databricks.verify: Insert a row with an old business date in test and check the gold total for that date changes.

checks.title: Facts arriving before their reference data
checks.question: What happens to a fact row whose customer, product or other reference record has not arrived yet?
checks.why: Orders for new products arrived hours before the product feed; an inner join silently dropped them, and the new-launch report showed zero sales on launch day.

evidence.looks_like: An "unknown" or placeholder member, or a quarantine with automatic reprocessing, and a step that re-points facts once the reference record arrives.

signals: Joins between facts and reference tables are described as inner joins with no handling of misses.
checks.fail_fast: Load a fact row whose reference key does not exist yet, then load the reference row; the fact must be kept and end up attached to the right reference record.

databricks.do: Insert an unknown-member row in each dimension and left join facts to it; or quarantine misses to a table and reprocess it in a scheduled task.
databricks.verify: An expectation or test counts facts pointing at the unknown member over time.

checks.title: Metric defined by name, not by formula
checks.question: Does every key metric have a complete definition: the formula, what is included and excluded, the grain, which date puts it in a period, the calendar used, the currency or unit and how amounts are converted? If two developers built it separately from the definition, would they get the same number?
checks.why: "Net sales" was defined as "sales minus returns". It did not say whether tax, discounts or shipping were included, or which exchange rate applied, so the number came out three different ways in three reports.

evidence.looks_like: A definition card per metric: formula, inclusions and exclusions, grain, the date that decides the period, calendar (fiscal or calendar), currency or unit and conversion rule, a worked example with real numbers, an owner and a sign-off date.

signals: Metrics are listed by name with a one-line description and no formula.
Definitions never mention tax, discounts, returns, cancellations, test accounts or currency.
No metric has a worked example with numbers.
checks.contradiction: Compare the metric definitions in the data model with the calculations described in report specifications or test cases: a calculation that adds a filter or rule the definition does not have means the definition is incomplete.
checks.fail_fast: Give the definition of one key metric to two people separately, ask each to calculate it from the same sample, and compare.

checks.title: Conflicting definitions across departments left hidden
checks.question: Have the departments that use the same term (customer, revenue, headcount, active) been asked for their definition, and are the differences written down and resolved, either into one definition or into clearly different names? When sales and finance show different numbers for the same word, has that argument already happened?
checks.why: Marketing counted an active customer as anyone who opened an email in ninety days; finance as anyone who paid in twelve months. The dashboard used finance's rule, marketing stopped trusting it, and built their own.

evidence.looks_like: For each shared term, the definition each department uses today, the differences, and the decision: one shared definition, or separate named measures (for example "booked revenue" and "invoiced revenue").

signals: Only one department was consulted on definitions that several departments use.
The same word appears in requirements from different teams with no note on whether it means the same.
No decision log entry records a resolved definition conflict.
checks.contradiction: Compare the stakeholder map with the definition sign-offs: a department that uses a term but did not sign its definition has not agreed to it.
checks.fail_fast: Email the top five terms to one person in each department that uses them, ask for their definition in one sentence, and put the answers side by side.

checks.title: Alerts reach someone who can act
checks.question: When a job fails, runs late or data looks wrong, who is alerted, through which channel, and within how long?
checks.why: Failure emails went to a shared mailbox nobody read; a load had failed for four days before a user asked why the report had not changed.

evidence.looks_like: Alerts for failure, lateness against the freshness target and data checks, routed to a named team or on-call rota, with an expected response time.

checks.fail_fast: Make a job fail in test and time how long it takes for a person to know.

databricks.do: Configure job notifications to a team channel or paging tool, plus duration-warning notifications for lateness.
databricks.verify: Fail a test job and time the alert.

checks.title: Jobs wait for their data, not the clock
checks.question: Does each job start when its upstream data is complete, rather than at a fixed time that assumes the upstream has finished?
checks.why: The report job ran at 06:00 assuming the load finished at 05:00; one night the load ran late, and the report published half a day's figures to the whole company.

evidence.looks_like: Dependencies declared between jobs or on completion markers, cross-team dependencies named, and what happens when an upstream is late.

signals: The schedule is a list of fixed times with no dependencies.
checks.fail_fast: Delay an upstream job in test and check that the downstream waits instead of running on stale or partial data.

databricks.do: Use task dependencies inside a job, and table-update or file-arrival triggers across jobs.
databricks.verify: Delay an upstream table in test and check the downstream job does not start.

checks.title: Restart after failing in the middle
checks.question: If a job fails halfway through writing, is the target left untouched or fully consistent, and can the job restart from the failed step without redoing everything?
checks.why: A job failed after updating three of five tables; reports joined new facts to old dimensions, and rerunning from the start re-applied the first three updates.

evidence.looks_like: Atomic writes per table, a defined restart point per step, consumers reading only completed runs, and a failure-injection test.

checks.fail_fast: Kill a job in test while it is writing, then restart it; outputs must match an uninterrupted run.

databricks.do: Each Delta write is atomic per table; split multi-table updates into tasks and use repair runs to rerun only failed tasks and those after them.
databricks.verify: Cancel a run mid-task in test, repair it, and compare outputs with a clean run.
databricks.traps: A repair reruns the whole failed task from the beginning, not from the failed row.

checks.title: Recovery time and data loss limits
checks.question: How quickly must the service recover after a major failure, how much data may be lost, and has recovery to those limits been tried?
checks.why: A storage account was deleted by mistake; the backups existed but nobody had tried a restore, and it took four days instead of the four hours the business assumed.

evidence.looks_like: An agreed recovery time and acceptable data loss, a backup or replication design that meets them, and the result of a restore test.

checks.fail_fast: Restore one important table from backup into a test environment and time it.

databricks.do: Decide which tables need deep clones or storage replication to another region; time travel is not a backup, because VACUUM removes old files.
databricks.verify: Restore a table from the chosen backup into a test catalog and time it.

checks.title: Stream restarts from where it stopped
checks.question: When a streaming job stops or is redeployed, does it resume from its saved position without losing or repeating data, and how is that state protected?
checks.why: A redeploy changed the stream's checkpoint location; the job restarted from the earliest available data, reprocessed a week and flooded downstream tables.

evidence.looks_like: Where progress is saved, how it survives redeploys and code changes, the source retention versus the longest expected outage, and a runbook for resetting a stream.

checks.fail_fast: Stop the stream for longer than a typical outage in test, redeploy a changed version, restart, and compare counts with the source.

databricks.do: Give every stream a fixed, environment-specific checkpoint location and keep it with the table; in Lakeflow pipelines checkpoints are managed for you.
databricks.verify: Redeploy a changed stream in test and confirm it resumes from its position.
databricks.traps: Some query changes are not allowed with an existing checkpoint (for example changes to stateful operations); plan a reset and backfill when they are needed.

checks.title: No named business owner for each data domain
checks.question: For each data domain the project uses (customer, product, finance, employee), is there a named business person who decides what the data means, what good quality is, and who may use it? When the team has a question about a field, who answers, and how long does it take?
checks.why: Product data had no business owner. Every question about categories went to the source system's technical team, who did not know, and the product hierarchy was argued about until the week before go-live.

evidence.looks_like: A table of data domains, each with a named business owner, a day-to-day steward if different, what they decide, and their agreement to the role.

signals: Data owners are listed as teams or systems rather than people.
The technical owner of a source system is named as the owner of the business meaning of its data.
Some domains in scope have no owner, or the owner is "to be confirmed".
checks.contradiction: Compare the data domains in the data model with the stakeholder map: a domain whose owner is not on the stakeholder map will not be consulted when its meaning is decided.
checks.fail_fast: List the domains and ask the sponsor to put one name against each in a ten-minute call, then ask each named person to confirm.

checks.title: Freshness target measured end to end
checks.question: What freshness or latency is promised (for example, ready by 07:00, or within one minute), and has the full path from source to consumer been timed against it?
checks.why: Each step met its own target, but source export, transfer, three layers and the report refresh added up to ninety minutes against a promised thirty.

evidence.looks_like: A freshness target per consumer, a time budget split across every hop, and a measured end to end time from the thin slice or a test run.

checks.fail_fast: Time one record from source change to visible in the report in the thin slice, and compare with the target.

checks.title: Tested at production volume
checks.question: Has the pipeline been run at production volume, including a peak day and the history load, before go-live?
checks.why: Every test ran on a tenth of the data; the first month-end in production ran out of memory in the biggest join and the finance close waited a day.

evidence.looks_like: A performance test at peak production volume with run times, compute size and cost recorded, and the result compared with the freshness target.

signals: The test strategy has no performance or volume test, or uses only small samples.
checks.fail_fast: Run the heaviest transformation on one full peak day of real (or realistically generated) data and time it.

databricks.do: Run on a production-sized copy (a deep clone in a test catalog, or generated data) on the production compute configuration; read the Spark UI or query profile for spill and skew.
databricks.verify: Record run time, compute size and cost from system.lakeflow.job_run_timeline and system.billing.usage.

checks.title: Dates set before the dependencies were known
checks.question: Were the milestones set after the dependencies (access, environments, source changes, other teams, approvals) were listed and confirmed with the people who own them? If the first milestone slips, will it be because of something outside the team that nobody had asked about?
checks.why: The go-live date was announced first. The source team's change freeze, the security review and the network change each added weeks, and none had been asked about when the date was set.

evidence.looks_like: A dependency list with each owner, the date they committed to, and the plan tasks that wait on it.

signals: Milestone dates appear in the brief or charter before any dependency list exists.
The plan has no dependencies, or lists them without owners or dates.
External teams named in the architecture do not appear in the plan.
checks.contradiction: Compare the architecture with the plan: every system or team the architecture relies on should appear as a dependency in the plan; one that does not is an unplanned wait.
checks.fail_fast: Phone the owner of the biggest external dependency and ask for the date they can deliver it, in writing.

checks.title: Risks listed, not managed
checks.question: Does each top risk have an owner, a trigger that tells us it is happening, a mitigation that is being done, and a date it was last reviewed? Looking back after a failure, will the cause be on the risk log with nothing done about it?
checks.why: "Source data quality may be poor" sat on the risk log for six months with no owner. It was exactly the reason the project missed its date.

evidence.looks_like: A short top-risks list where each risk has an owner, a trigger, a mitigation with a due date, and a recent review date.

signals: Risks with no owner, or with a team rather than a person as owner.
No triggers or mitigation actions, only descriptions.
The risk log has not changed in several weeks while status reports describe new problems.
checks.contradiction: Compare the RAID log with status reports: problems in the status reports that were never on the risk log, or risks that became issues without the log changing, mean the log is not used.
checks.fail_fast: Take the top three risks and ask each owner what they did about it this week.

checks.title: Decisions not written down
checks.question: Is there a decision log recording the options, the choice, the reason, who decided and when? When a decision is reopened by someone who was not in the room, what will we show them?
checks.why: The team agreed to keep only the latest customer address. Three months later a new manager asked why history was missing, and with no record the decision was reversed and the work redone.

evidence.looks_like: A decision log or short decision records: context, options, decision, reason, owner, who signed, date.

signals: No decision log or decision records exist among the project documents.
Meeting notes contain "agreed" or "decided" but no decision log entry matches.
Architecture choices are stated with no record of the options considered.
checks.contradiction: Compare meeting notes or status reports with the decision log: a decision mentioned in notes but not in the log is one that can be lost.
checks.fail_fast: List the last five important choices from memory and check how many are in the log.

checks.title: Green until it is red
checks.question: Do status reports show amber or red when something is slipping, with the reason and the next step? If the project fails suddenly, will the reports from the month before have shown it as green?
checks.why: Status stayed green for four months while the team quietly fell behind. It went red two weeks before go-live, when there was nothing left to do but move the date.

evidence.looks_like: Status reports where the colour is based on stated rules (for example forecast versus baseline), and where amber appears early with a recovery action.

signals: Every status report is green.
The status colour does not change while the forecast date or open issues change.
No forecast finish date, only activities done.
checks.contradiction: Compare status reports with the RAID log and the estimate: a green status alongside rising issues, a rate below the estimate, or slipping dependencies means the colour is not telling the truth.
checks.fail_fast: Write down the rule for red, amber and green today and apply it to the last report.

checks.title: Testing and deployment left to the end
checks.question: Does the plan have testing and deployment to a production-like environment starting in the first weeks of build, rather than after it? If go-live slips, will it be because the first real deployment happened a month before the date?
checks.why: Everything was built, then tested, then deployed. The first deployment found network, permission and performance problems that took longer to fix than the build had taken.

evidence.looks_like: A test strategy and a release approach agreed in discovery, a first deployment of a thin slice in the first weeks, and "done" defined as tested and deployed.

signals: No test strategy or deployment document exists, or it says "to be defined".
The plan has testing and deployment as single phases after build.
The definition of done mentions coding but not testing or deployment.
checks.contradiction: Compare the plan with the test strategy: if the strategy describes continuous testing but the plan has one test phase at the end, the plan wins and testing will be squeezed.
checks.fail_fast: Deploy the thin slice to the test environment this week, through the real release route.

checks.title: Access and environments treated as admin
checks.question: Were access to sources, environments and tools requested in the first week and tracked as dependencies with owners and dates? If the build starts late, will it be because the team waited weeks for access?
checks.why: Access requests were raised when build started. Approvals took six weeks, so the team spent the first sprints on paper designs that the real data later contradicted.

evidence.looks_like: A list of every access and environment request with the date raised, the approver, the expected date and its current state.

signals: No access or environment requests are listed in the plan or RAID log.
Access is described as "assumed" or "will be arranged".
Discovery has no real data extract because access had not arrived.
checks.contradiction: Compare the plan's start of build with the access request dates: a build that starts before access is expected is planned to wait.
checks.fail_fast: Raise every access request today and record the date each one arrives.

checks.title: History load not on the plan as real tasks
checks.question: Is the history load on the plan as its own tasks, with the elapsed time it needs (source extract windows, several trial runs, checking the old numbers), not folded into "build"? If go-live slips, will it be because the history load turned out to be a project of its own?
checks.why: The plan gave the history load two days before go-live. The source could only be read at night, the first run found years with a different code list, and the full load took five weekends.

evidence.looks_like: Plan tasks for the history extract, at least one full trial run, checking the old periods with the business and the final load, each with elapsed time, source windows and an owner.

signals: The history load appears only in the architecture, not in the plan.
The plan has one task, or a few days, for loading many years of history.
No trial run of the history load is planned before the cut-over.
checks.contradiction: Compare the history load approach in the architecture or deployment plan with the plan's tasks: an approach that needs night windows and several runs, given a couple of days in the plan, will slip.
checks.fail_fast: Time a full extract of one year of history from the source now and multiply by the years in scope.

checks.title: Data fixes with no owner and no time
checks.question: When profiling or testing finds bad data at the source (missing keys, wrong codes, duplicate customers), is it agreed who fixes it, where (at the source, by the business, or in the pipeline), and is that time on someone's plan? Whose plan holds the weeks of cleansing that the profile is already hinting at?
checks.why: Profiling showed that a fifth of customers had no region. Everyone assumed someone else would fix it; the business had no time booked, and user acceptance failed on regional totals six weeks before go-live.

evidence.looks_like: A data issues list from profiling, each with the decision on where it is fixed, an owner, the effort, and matching tasks in the project plan or the source team's plan.

signals: The data profile lists quality problems that appear nowhere in the plan or RAID log.
Fixes are assigned to "the business" or "the source" with no name or date.
No time for data fixing appears in the plan.
checks.contradiction: Compare the data profile or data quality findings with the plan: each problem that needs fixing, with no task and owner, is work that will appear in user acceptance instead.
checks.fail_fast: Take the top five data problems from the profile and get a named owner and a date for each this week.

checks.title: Reconciliation and user acceptance planned as one pass
checks.question: Does the plan allow for more than one cycle of reconciliation and user acceptance (test, find differences, explain or fix, test again), with business time booked for each cycle? If the first round finds the numbers do not match, is there any time left to fix them?
checks.why: One week of user acceptance was planned. The first day showed revenue three percent off the ledger, the explanation took two weeks, and there was no second test window before the go-live date.

evidence.looks_like: At least two reconciliation and acceptance cycles on the plan, with time between them to explain and fix differences, and business testers booked for each.

signals: The plan has a single user acceptance window.
Reconciliation is not a task in the plan, or sits inside "testing".
No time between the end of user acceptance and go-live.
checks.contradiction: Compare the test strategy's reconciliation approach with the plan: a strategy that compares every layer with trusted figures, given one short window, will run out of time on the first difference.
checks.fail_fast: Reconcile one month of one key number against the business's trusted figure now and time how long it takes.

checks.title: Cut-over weekend not planned
checks.question: Is there an hour-by-hour cut-over plan covering the business freeze, the final loads, the checks before users are let in, the point after which there is no going back, the rollback steps, and who is on call? At three in the morning on cut-over night, if the final load fails, who decides what happens next?
checks.why: Cut-over was "the weekend after UAT". The final history load overran by ten hours, nobody had agreed a point to stop, and on Monday half the users saw new numbers while the rest still had the old reports.

evidence.looks_like: A cut-over runbook with timed steps and owners, the business freeze window, checks before opening to users, a go-back deadline and rollback steps, a call list, and at least one rehearsal.

signals: No cut-over plan, or one line saying "deploy to production".
No business freeze, rollback window or decision point is mentioned.
No rehearsal of the cut-over is planned.
checks.contradiction: Compare the cut-over plan's timings with the history load and final load run times measured in test: a window shorter than the measured loads will overrun.
checks.fail_fast: Write the cut-over as timed steps on one page and add up the hours against the window you have.

checks.title: Use of personal data not confirmed as allowed
checks.question: For each use of personal data in the requirements, has the business confirmed with its privacy or legal team that the use is allowed: the purpose, any consent it depends on, and who may see it? If the privacy team stops the project a month before go-live, will it be over a use nobody asked them about?
checks.why: The marketing dashboard joined customer purchases to support-call notes. Customers had never been told their call notes would be used for marketing, and the privacy officer stopped the release in user testing.

evidence.looks_like: A list of the personal data each requirement needs, the business purpose, the basis that allows it (consent, contract, legal duty), who may see it, and the privacy team's recorded answer.

signals: Requirements need customer, employee or patient data with no mention of purpose or permission.
The privacy or legal team is not on the stakeholder map.
Personal data is treated only as a security or masking question.
checks.contradiction: Compare the personal data named in the requirements with the stakeholder map and decision log: personal data in use with no privacy sign-off recorded is a go-live blocker waiting to be found.
checks.fail_fast: Send the privacy team a one-page list of the personal data and its purposes this week and ask for a yes, a no or a condition.

checks.title: Counts and totals reconciled layer by layer
checks.question: Are row counts and key totals compared automatically between the source and each layer on every load, with the differences explained?
checks.why: The report was four percent short of the source and nobody could say in which layer rows had been lost, so a week went into tracing one join that dropped orphan rows.

evidence.looks_like: Counts and sums of key measures captured at the source and after each layer for every run, stored, compared, and every expected difference (filters, quarantined rows) accounted for.

signals: Reconciliation appears only as a one-off test activity, not as part of every run.
checks.fail_fast: For one day of real data, write down the source count and total, then the count and total in each layer, and explain every difference.

databricks.do: Write per-run counts and sums per layer to a reconciliation table from each task; DESCRIBE HISTORY operationMetrics give rows written per commit.
databricks.verify: A dashboard or query compares source and each layer per run.

checks.title: Matched against a number the business already trusts
checks.question: Are the final numbers checked against an independent figure the business already trusts (a finance ledger, an existing report, a source application screen)?
checks.why: Source-to-target counts all matched, yet the new revenue figure disagreed with the finance ledger because the definition of revenue differed; it was found only at user acceptance.

evidence.looks_like: A named trusted figure for each key measure, the comparison method, and an agreed explanation of known differences.

checks.fail_fast: Ask the business owner which existing number they would compare against, and compare one month of thin-slice output with it now.

checks.title: First production loads reconciled
checks.question: Were the first production loads, including the history load, reconciled against the source and trusted figures before users were told to rely on them?
checks.why: Production used a different source instance with extra test records; nobody reconciled the first loads, and dummy orders appeared in the board pack.

evidence.looks_like: A reconciliation result for each of the first production runs, with sign-off, recorded in the hypercare or go-live report.

checks.fail_fast: Add "reconcile first production load" as a go-live checklist item with an owner and a tolerance.

checks.title: Everything that runs is in version control
checks.question: Is everything that runs in production (pipeline code, SQL, job definitions, schedules, data quality rules, permissions) kept in version control?
checks.why: The schedule and parameters were edited by hand in the production interface; when the job was recreated after an incident, nobody knew the real settings and it ran with wrong ones for a week.

evidence.looks_like: A repository layout that includes code, job and schedule definitions and configuration, and a rule that production is never changed by hand.

signals: Jobs are described as "configured in the user interface".
checks.fail_fast: Pick one production job and try to recreate it in a fresh environment only from the repository.

databricks.do: Keep code in Git folders and jobs, pipelines and schedules as bundle resources in the repository.
databricks.verify: Recreate a job from the repository into an empty workspace with a bundle deploy.
databricks.traps: Jobs edited in the UI drift from the bundle; restrict edit rights in production.

checks.title: Automated promotion of the same build
