checks.question: Is the same tested build promoted automatically from development to test to production, with an approval step before production?
checks.why: Each environment was deployed by copying scripts by hand; production ended up with an older version of one script, and test results said nothing about what really ran.

evidence.looks_like: A pipeline that builds once, deploys the same version to each environment with environment settings injected, and records which version is where.

checks.fail_fast: Deploy the thin slice to test using only the pipeline, with nobody clicking in the target environment.

databricks.do: Use Declarative Automation Bundles with one target per environment; CI runs databricks bundle validate and deploy with a service principal.
databricks.verify: The production deployment history shows only the CI service principal deploying.

checks.title: No secrets in the repository
checks.question: Are passwords, keys and tokens kept in a secret store and read at run time, never in code, configuration files or the repository's history?
checks.why: A database password was committed in a script; the repository was later shared with a vendor, and the security team had to rotate credentials across four systems.

evidence.looks_like: A named secret store per environment, code that reads secrets by name, and an automated secret scan on the repository.

checks.fail_fast: Run a secret scanner over the whole repository history today.

databricks.do: Keep secrets in secret scopes (optionally backed by the cloud key store) and read them with dbutils.secrets; prefer Unity Catalog connections and service credentials over passwords in code.
databricks.traps: Secrets printed in a notebook cell are redacted, but derived strings and logs can still leak them.

checks.title: Rolling back a release, including its data
checks.question: If a release goes wrong, how are both the code and any data or table structure it changed put back, and has that been rehearsed?
checks.why: A release changed a table's structure and backfilled it; the code could be rolled back in minutes, but the data could not, and reports were broken for two days.

evidence.looks_like: A rollback plan per release covering code, schema and data (restore points or table versions), and a rehearsal in a production-like environment.

signals: The cut-over plan has no rollback section, or says "roll back the code" only.
checks.fail_fast: Deploy a release that changes a table in test, then roll it back fully, and time it.

databricks.do: Use RESTORE TABLE ... TO VERSION AS OF for data rollback, within the retention window; redeploy the previous bundle version for code.
databricks.verify: Rehearse RESTORE on a test table after a schema-changing release.
databricks.traps: RESTORE only works for versions VACUUM has not cleaned up.

checks.title: Vague words in the requirements
checks.question: Has every vague word in the requirements, such as "real-time", "fast", "all data", "user-friendly", "accurate" or "complete", been replaced with a number or a test? If the users reject the system at the end, will it be because we each read those words differently?
checks.why: "Real-time" meant within a second to the sponsor and by the next morning to the team. The design was built for daily loads and had to be rebuilt late in the project.

evidence.looks_like: Every quality word paired with a measure, for example "available by 7 a.m. on working days" instead of "timely", or "the last three years" instead of "all history".

signals: Words such as real-time, near real-time, fast, quickly, timely, all data, complete, accurate, user-friendly, intuitive, seamless, scalable or robust appear without a number next to them.
Lists of required data or reports end with "etc." or "and so on".
checks.contradiction: Compare the requirements with the architecture: if the requirement says "real-time" and the architecture schedules a daily batch, someone's reading of the word is wrong.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the requester to put a number on each vague word in a fifteen-minute call, and write the answers down.

checks.title: No acceptance criteria
checks.question: Does every requirement have acceptance criteria that the data can be tested against? At user acceptance, how will we and the business agree that a requirement is met?
checks.why: Requirements said "show monthly sales by region". At user acceptance the business compared it with their own report, got a different number, and nobody had agreed in advance which one was right.

evidence.looks_like: For each requirement, one or more criteria in the form "given this data, the result is this", ideally with a known figure the business already trusts.

signals: Requirements or user stories have no "acceptance criteria" or "done when" section.
Acceptance criteria repeat the requirement in other words rather than describing a test.
Backlog items are marked ready for build without criteria.
checks.contradiction: Compare the requirements with the test strategy: requirements that have no matching test, or tests that trace to no requirement, show the two were written apart.
checks.fail_fast: Take the three most important requirements and write a test for each with the business owner, using a figure from a report they already trust.

checks.title: Business definitions not agreed and signed
checks.question: Are the key business definitions (for example revenue, active customer, order date) written down and signed by the person who owns each one? If two departments see different numbers after go-live, which signed definition settles it?
checks.why: Sales counted revenue when the order was booked; finance counted it when it was paid. Both signed the requirements, which said "revenue", and the dashboard was disowned by one of them in the first week.

evidence.looks_like: A definitions list with the exact rule for each term, the grain, the owner who signed it and the date.

signals: The data dictionary has names but no rules, owners or sign-off.
The same term is used in requirements from different departments with no definition.
Definitions are marked "to be confirmed" in a document that has passed discovery sign-off.
checks.contradiction: Compare the requirements with the data model: if a term in the requirements has a different rule, or no rule, in the data model, the definition was never agreed.
checks.fail_fast: Ask two of the main consumers to write their own definition of the top five terms separately, then compare the answers.

checks.title: Requirements written without looking at the data
checks.question: Were the requirements checked against a profile of the real source data? If a requirement turns out to be impossible, will we find out in discovery or in testing?
checks.why: The requirement asked for sales by product category. The source had no category for a third of products, which only came to light when the report was tested.

evidence.looks_like: A data profile per source (volumes, keys, nulls, odd values) and a note against each requirement saying which source fields support it and any gaps found.

signals: No data profiling section or results in the discovery document.
Requirements name fields or attributes that do not appear in any source description.
Phrases such as "data to be confirmed" or "assumed available" against required fields.
checks.contradiction: Compare the requirements with the data model or source mapping: a required field with no source mapped to it is a requirement nobody checked against the data.
checks.fail_fast: Pull one real extract from each source and map the top ten requirements to actual columns in an afternoon.

checks.title: Non-functional needs missing
checks.question: Are freshness, volume and growth, recovery time and acceptable data loss, retention, and who may see what written as requirements with numbers? If the system works but is rejected, will it be because it is too slow, too stale, or unrecoverable?
checks.why: Nobody asked how fresh the data had to be or how quickly it had to recover. After the first overnight failure the business found out it would take a day to recover, and the system was not accepted.

evidence.looks_like: A short non-functional list: freshness deadline, expected volume and growth, how long it may be down, how much data may be lost, how long data is kept, and access rules.

signals: No "non-functional" heading in the requirements.
Freshness, recovery or retention are mentioned only as "to be agreed".
Volume is described in words ("large") rather than numbers.
checks.contradiction: Compare the requirements with the runbook or support model: if the runbook promises recovery within hours but no requirement says what is needed, or the reverse, the two disagree on what was promised.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the business owner: "If this is down for a day, what happens?" and write down the answer as a number.

checks.title: Everything is a "must"
checks.question: Are the requirements prioritised (for example must, should, could and won't), with real items in the "won't" list and fewer musts than the first release can deliver? If time runs out, has the business already said which requirements go first?
checks.why: Every one of sixty requirements was marked essential. When the build ran late the team cut by effort instead of value, dropped the one report the finance director actually used, and the release was rejected.

evidence.looks_like: Each requirement with a priority agreed by the business owner, a "won't this time" list with real items in it, and the musts sized to fit the first release with room to spare.

signals: No priority column in the requirements, or every requirement has the same priority.
The "won't" or "not this release" list is empty.
Musts make up most of the requirements.
checks.contradiction: Compare the must-have requirements with the first release in the plan: musts that are not in the first release, or a first release full of shoulds and coulds, mean priority and plan disagree.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the business owner: "If we could deliver only five of these, which five?" and record the answer as the priority.

checks.title: Capacity counted in people, not in real hours
checks.question: Does the plan use each person's real availability: their share of time on this project, planned leave, public holidays, other commitments and support duties? If the team delivers two thirds of what was planned, will the missing third be leave and part-time allocations nobody subtracted?
checks.why: The plan assumed five full-time developers. Two were shared with production support, one had three weeks of leave in the summer, and the real capacity was barely three people, so the first MVP slipped a month.

evidence.looks_like: A team table with each named person, their percentage on the project, known leave and the weeks they are needed, with the total compared against the effort in the estimate.

signals: The plan lists roles or head counts with no names or percentages.
No mention of leave, holidays or support duties.
The same person is allocated full time on this project and another one.
checks.contradiction: Compare the estimate's effort with the plan's available hours: if effort divided by real capacity gives a later date than the plan shows, the plan assumes people who do not exist.
checks.fail_fast: Add up each person's real available days for the next eight weeks and compare them with the planned work.

checks.title: Source experts' time never booked
checks.question: Is the time the project needs from source system experts (to explain tables, deletes and odd values, to review mappings and to fix extracts) agreed with their manager, in hours per week and by date? When the team needs an answer about the source, how long will it wait?
checks.why: The only person who understood the source's status codes worked on that system's own release. She gave the project an hour a week when she could, and every mapping question waited ten days for an answer.

evidence.looks_like: Named source experts with agreed hours per week through discovery, build and test, confirmed by their line manager, and a deputy for each.

signals: Source experts are named in the stakeholder map with no time commitment.
Open questions about source data stay open across several status reports.
The plan relies on "input from the source team" without names or dates.
checks.contradiction: Compare the number of sources in the architecture with the expert time booked in the plan: a source with no booked expert will be understood by guessing.
checks.fail_fast: Ask each source expert's manager to confirm, in writing, the hours per week they will give the project.

checks.title: Business testers and sign-off people not booked
checks.question: Are the business users who will test, reconcile numbers and sign off named, with their days booked and clear of month-end, year-end and their own peak periods? If user acceptance slips, will it be because the testers were closing the books that week?
checks.why: User acceptance was planned for the last week of the quarter. Every finance tester was on the quarter close, the test window passed with a handful of cases run, and go-live moved by six weeks.

evidence.looks_like: Named testers and approvers, the days each has agreed to give, their managers' agreement, and a test window checked against the business calendar.

signals: The test strategy says "business users" without names.
User acceptance dates fall in a month-end, quarter-end or year-end period.
No business manager has agreed to release testers.
checks.contradiction: Compare the plan's user acceptance window with the business calendar or the testers' own commitments: a window that overlaps their busiest week will not get the testing it needs.
checks.fail_fast: Ask each named tester's manager to put the test days in their calendar now.

checks.title: Go or no-go decided on the day, not agreed in advance
checks.question: Are the go-live criteria (reconciled numbers within tolerance, no open critical defects, support ready, users trained, rollback rehearsed) written down and agreed with the business owner before the go or no-go meeting? If the history load finishes with two regions unreconciled, do we already know whether we go?
checks.why: With no agreed criteria, the go or no-go meeting became a debate. The sponsor wanted the date, the test lead wanted another week, and they went live with known differences that took three months to explain away.

evidence.looks_like: A go or no-go checklist agreed weeks before cut-over, with each criterion, the evidence for it, who confirms it, and what happens if it fails (delay, go with a workaround, or partial release).

signals: No go-live criteria are written, or they say "UAT signed off".
The go or no-go decision has no named decider.
Criteria do not mention reconciliation, support readiness or rollback.
checks.contradiction: Compare the go-live criteria with the test results and defect list on the decision date: a go decision taken while a criterion was unmet means the criteria were not the real basis.
checks.fail_fast: Draft the go-live checklist now and ask the business owner which line they would refuse to go without.

checks.title: Consumers outside the steering group not told
checks.question: Have all consumers of the data being replaced or changed been found and told, including other teams' extracts, downstream systems and spreadsheets fed from the old source, not only the users in the steering group? Who will discover our go-live because their own report broke?
checks.why: The old warehouse table was replaced. A pricing team nobody had met read it every night for their own model, and their prices were wrong for three days before anyone linked it to the release.

evidence.looks_like: A consumer list built from access logs and lineage, not only interviews, each consumer told the change and the date, and their confirmation recorded.

signals: The consumer list comes only from the steering group and requirements workshops.
No one has checked who reads the tables or feeds being replaced.
No notice period for consumers is in the deployment plan.
checks.contradiction: Compare the consumers in the stakeholder map with the readers found in access logs or lineage: a reader who is not on the map has not been told.
checks.fail_fast: Pull the last ninety days of reads on the tables being replaced and contact every reader not on the map.

checks.title: Business rules written as prose, not as testable rules
checks.question: Is every business rule (how a customer is classified, when an order counts, how a discount is applied) written as a precise rule with at least one worked example of input and expected result? If a tester and a developer read the rule separately, would they agree on the answer for a tricky case?
checks.why: The rule said "VIP customers get priority". Nobody wrote down that VIP meant spend over a threshold in the last twelve rolling months, so developers used the calendar year and a fifth of VIPs were missing.

evidence.looks_like: Each rule numbered, stated as a condition and a result, with two or three worked examples using real values, including at least one edge case, and the person who confirmed it.

signals: Rules are embedded in long paragraphs rather than listed and numbered.
Rules have no examples, or only the obvious case.
Words such as "usually", "normally", "where appropriate" or "as needed" appear in rules.
checks.contradiction: Compare the business rules in the requirements with the test cases: a rule with no test, or a test that checks something no rule states, shows the rules were never made testable.
checks.fail_fast: Pick the three most complex rules and ask the business owner to work one real record through each by hand.

checks.title: What the user sees when data is bad or missing not decided by the business
checks.question: When a value is missing, a record fails a check, or a source is late, what should the user see: a blank, a placeholder such as "unknown", yesterday's figure, a warning, or nothing at all? Has the business chosen, for each key report? If a manager makes a decision on incomplete data, will the report have told them?
checks.why: A store's sales file failed to load. The dashboard showed the store at zero without any warning, and a regional manager phoned the store manager to ask why nothing had been sold.

evidence.looks_like: For each key report or consumer, what is shown for missing values, rejected rows, late sources and partial periods, agreed with the users, with how they are told the data is incomplete.

signals: The requirements describe only the happy path.
Rules for bad data exist in the technical design but not in the requirements.
Words such as "unknown", "missing", "incomplete", "partial" or "late" never appear in the requirements.
checks.contradiction: Compare the requirements with the data quality design: if the design quarantines or drops rows but the requirements never say what users should see when that happens, users will see silent gaps.
checks.fail_fast: Show users a mock-up of a key report with one region missing and ask what they expect it to look like.

checks.title: History rows stay correct on reruns and out-of-order changes
checks.question: Does the history logic (effective from and to dates, current flag) stay correct when a load is rerun, when two changes arrive in one batch, or when changes arrive out of order?
checks.why: A rerun closed and reopened every current row, and an older change arriving late became "current", so customers showed last year's address with overlapping validity periods.

evidence.looks_like: Changes ordered by a source sequence or change timestamp, not arrival time; a hash to skip unchanged rows; and tests for rerun, two-changes-per-batch and out-of-order cases.

checks.fail_fast: Feed three versions of one record in reverse order, then rerun the same batch; exactly one current row and no overlapping date ranges may remain.

databricks.do: Prefer AUTO CDC ... STORED AS SCD TYPE 2 with SEQUENCE BY on a source sequence; it places out-of-order changes in the right history position. Hand-written MERGE needs a hash of tracked columns and ordering by sequence.
databricks.verify: Feed reversed versions and a rerun in test; check no overlapping __START_AT / __END_AT ranges.
databricks.traps: Sequencing by ingestion time instead of a source sequence breaks history when changes arrive out of order.

checks.title: A column renamed, removed or retyped
checks.question: When a source renames, removes or changes the type of a column, does the pipeline stop loudly before writing wrong data?
checks.why: A source changed an amount column from cents to a decimal in dollars; the pipeline cast it happily and revenue fell a hundredfold in the morning report.

evidence.looks_like: An expected schema checked on every load, breaking changes failing the load with a clear alert, and range or distribution checks on key measures.

checks.fail_fast: In test, rename one column and change one type in a source sample; the load must fail with a message that names the column.

databricks.do: Supply an explicit schema or schema hints for critical columns; let Delta schema enforcement reject mismatched writes; add CHECK constraints for ranges.
databricks.verify: A test file with a renamed or retyped column fails the load with a clear error.
databricks.traps: Type mismatches can land in _rescued_data quietly; alert when that column is not null.

checks.title: Scope written only as "in"
checks.question: Is there a written list of what is out of scope, as well as what is in? When someone says "I assumed that was included", which document will we point to?
checks.why: The scope listed the tables to build. The business assumed the reports on top were included too, and the argument cost a month and the sponsor's trust.

evidence.looks_like: Three lists, in scope, out of scope and later, each item specific enough that a stranger could say which list a new request belongs to.

signals: No "out of scope" heading or list in the discovery, scope or requirements document.
The out-of-scope list is generic ("anything not listed above").
checks.contradiction: Compare the scope with the requirements: a requirement that is neither in the in-scope list nor explicitly out is a future argument.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the business owner to read only the out-of-scope list and say which item surprises them.

checks.title: The data scope traps left silent
checks.question: Has each of the ten data scope traps been written down as in, out or later: history and backfill, deletes at the source, late and corrected data, changes over time, bad rows, source data quality, personal data, reports and dashboards, access and onboarding, and recovery? Which of them will someone assume was included?
checks.why: Nobody wrote down whether deleted customers should disappear from the reports. The business assumed yes, the team assumed no, and the gap was found by an auditor.

evidence.looks_like: A table with one row per trap, the decision (in, out or later), who decided and why.

signals: Several of the words history, backfill, delete, late, correction, bad rows, quality, personal data, reports, access and recovery do not appear in the scope section.
Traps are mentioned but marked "to be confirmed" after discovery sign-off.
checks.contradiction: Compare the scope with the architecture: a trap the architecture handles (for example history kept) that the scope does not mention, or the reverse, shows the two were never reconciled.
checks.fail_fast: Walk the ten traps with the business owner in thirty minutes and record each answer.

checks.title: Scope creep with no change process
checks.question: Is there an agreed way to handle a new request: who can raise it, how it is sized, who decides, and how the plan and estimate change? If the project ends late, how much of the lateness will be work that was added without anyone deciding to add it?
checks.why: Each request was small and agreed in a meeting. After three months, a fifth of the work had never been estimated, the date had not moved, and the team was blamed for the slip.

evidence.looks_like: A written change process and a change log where each change shows the request, its size, its effect on date and cost, the decision and who made it.

signals: No "change control", "change request" or "change process" in the plan.
Status reports mention new items that do not appear in the original scope or in any change log.
Meeting notes include "can we also add" with no follow-up decision.
checks.contradiction: Compare the latest status report or backlog with the signed scope: items in the backlog that are not in the scope and have no change record are unmanaged creep.
checks.fail_fast: Count backlog items added since sign-off and check how many have a recorded decision.

checks.title: Personal and sensitive data found and classified
checks.question: Which columns hold personal or sensitive data, in which sources and layers, and is each classified?
checks.why: Free-text notes held customer phone numbers and health details; nobody had classified them, so they were copied unmasked into a table hundreds of analysts could read.

evidence.looks_like: A classification for every column in scope (public, internal, confidential, personal, special category), including free-text fields, recorded in the data dictionary or catalog.

signals: Personal data is not mentioned, or mentioned only as "will follow policy".
checks.fail_fast: Scan a real extract of each source for patterns like emails, phone numbers and national ids, including in free-text columns.

databricks.do: Apply governed tags for classification on columns in Unity Catalog; data classification can suggest tags.
databricks.verify: Query information_schema column tags to list sensitive columns and their owners.

checks.title: Who can see what
checks.question: Who may see which tables, rows and columns, and how is that enforced (masking, row filters, separate views) rather than trusted?
checks.why: Regional managers were meant to see only their own region, but the report filtered it in the front end; anyone querying the table directly saw every region's salaries.

evidence.looks_like: An access matrix by group, enforced in the data platform itself with masking and row-level rules, and tests that run as each persona.

checks.fail_fast: Log in as a test user of the lowest-privilege persona and query the most sensitive table directly.

databricks.do: Grant to groups in Unity Catalog; apply row filters and column masks, or ABAC policies on governed tags at catalog or schema level for many tables.
databricks.verify: Query the table as a test user from the lowest persona.
databricks.traps: Row filters and masks need recent runtimes (older compute returns no data), cannot be put on views, and block time travel and clones on that table.

checks.title: Retention and the right to be forgotten
checks.question: How long is each kind of data kept, and how is a person's data erased everywhere it lives, including history tables, old table versions, backups and extracts?
checks.why: A customer's erasure request deleted their current row, but the history table, old file versions kept for recovery and a weekly extract to a partner still held their data.

evidence.looks_like: A retention period per data class, an erasure procedure that covers every layer, history, versions and copies, and the time it takes to complete.

checks.fail_fast: Trace one test person through every table, version and extract in test and count where their data would remain after the erasure procedure.

databricks.do: DELETE the person's rows in every layer, then VACUUM so old files are removed; deletion vectors need a REORG ... APPLY (PURGE) before VACUUM to physically remove rows.
databricks.verify: After the procedure, time travel to an earlier version and confirm the data is gone once retention has passed.
databricks.traps: Time travel, deep clones and exports keep copies until each is cleaned too.

checks.title: A contract with each consumer
checks.question: For each consumer (report, extract, application, model), is there an agreed contract: the tables or fields they use, their meaning, grain, freshness and how they will receive it?
checks.why: A downstream team built a pricing model on an internal staging table; a routine refactor renamed it and the pricing model failed on a sale day.

evidence.looks_like: A list of consumers and, for each, the published interface, its fields and meaning, grain, freshness promise and a named contact.

signals: Consumers are listed by name only, with no interface or freshness.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the main consumer which exact fields they will read; check each is in the data model with a definition.

checks.title: Business definitions live in one place
checks.question: Is each business measure (revenue, active customer) defined and calculated once, in a shared model, rather than separately in each report?
checks.why: Three dashboards calculated margin three ways; the leadership meeting spent an hour arguing about which number was right instead of deciding anything.

evidence.looks_like: A definitions list with the owner of each measure, implemented once in a shared model or semantic layer that reports reuse.

checks.fail_fast: Ask two consumers to write down how they calculate the top measure; compare the answers.

databricks.do: Define shared measures once as Unity Catalog metric views and point dashboards and Genie spaces at them.
databricks.traps: Metric views are newer; check the feature's status in your workspace before standardising on it.

checks.title: Only the sponsor is managed
checks.question: Does the stakeholder map include the people outside the weekly meeting who can block go-live: source system owners, operations, security, the platform team and downstream users? Who could stop this project in its last month that we have not spoken to in its first?
checks.why: The sponsor was kept happy every week. Security saw the design for the first time two weeks before go-live, required personal data to be masked, and the release slipped by two months.

evidence.looks_like: A stakeholder map naming each person or group, what they care about, what they can approve or block, when they were last spoken to, and how they are kept informed.

signals: No stakeholder map or communication plan exists.
The map lists only the sponsor, the business owner and the project team.
Operations, security, source owners or downstream consumers are not named anywhere.
checks.contradiction: Compare the architecture with the stakeholder map: every source, platform and consumer in the architecture has an owner who should appear on the map; one who does not is an unmanaged blocker.
checks.fail_fast: List everyone who must say yes before go-live and book a thirty-minute meeting with each one you have not met.

checks.title: Nobody clearly owns the decisions
checks.question: For each kind of decision (scope, definitions, priorities, go-live), is one named person the decision owner? When two senior people disagree, who decides, and how long will we wait?
checks.why: Two directors each believed they owned the project. Every decision was taken twice, the team built to whichever spoke last, and both rejected the result.

evidence.looks_like: A responsibility table (who decides, who is consulted, who is informed) for the main decision types, with one decider per type and a route for escalation.

signals: No responsibility table, or several people marked as the decider for the same thing.
Decision log entries with no named decider.
Phrases such as "the business will decide" without a name.
checks.contradiction: Compare the stakeholder map with the decision log: decisions signed by someone the map does not name as the decider are likely to be reopened.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the sponsor to name, in writing, the one person who decides on scope and definitions.

checks.title: No real numbers shown to the business
checks.question: Have the business users seen real numbers from real data, regularly, before user acceptance testing? If they say "these numbers are wrong" at the end, will it be the first time they have looked?
checks.why: Demos used made-up data that looked fine. The first time the business saw real numbers was user acceptance, and they did not recognise them.

evidence.looks_like: Regular demos, roughly every two weeks, with real data, and a record of what the business said and what changed as a result.

signals: No demos are planned or recorded before the test stage.
Demos are described as using sample, dummy or mock data.
The data profile was not shown to the business owner during discovery.
checks.contradiction: Compare the plan with the meeting notes or status reports: planned demos that do not appear in the notes did not happen.
checks.fail_fast: Show the business owner one real number from the thin slice and ask whether they recognise it.

checks.title: Test levels that include data tests
checks.question: Does the test strategy cover code tests, data tests (rules, reconciliation), integration end to end, performance and user acceptance, each with an owner?
checks.why: Tests checked that each function worked on hand-made rows; nobody tested the real data end to end, and the first integrated run produced reports nobody recognised.

evidence.looks_like: A test strategy naming each test level, what it proves, who runs it, where, and with what data, including data quality and reconciliation tests.

signals: The test strategy says "to be defined", or covers only unit tests and user acceptance.
checks.fail_fast: For each top requirement, write the one data test that would prove it, and see which ones you cannot write.

checks.title: Realistic, safe test data
checks.question: Where does test data come from, is it realistic enough to find real problems (volumes, edge cases, bad rows), and is personal data masked or synthetic?
checks.why: Test data was a tidy hand-made sample with no nulls or duplicates; every test passed, and the first real load failed on problems the sample could never have shown.

evidence.looks_like: A source of test data per environment (masked copy, sampled production, generated), the edge cases it includes, and security approval.

checks.fail_fast: Compare the null, duplicate and orphan-key rates of the test data with the real-data profile.

databricks.do: Use shallow or deep clones of masked production tables into a test catalog, or generated data.
databricks.traps: Clones of tables with row filters or masks are not supported; mask before cloning.

checks.title: Users test with numbers they recognise
checks.question: Will business users accept the solution by checking real numbers they know, against agreed criteria, rather than by looking at screens?
checks.why: User acceptance was a demo of the dashboard layout; the first time finance compared it with their own numbers was after go-live, and they rejected it.

evidence.looks_like: User acceptance scenarios with expected figures supplied by the business, named testers, dates, and sign-off criteria.

checks.fail_fast: Ask the business owner for three numbers they know by heart and check them in the thin slice.

checks.title: Failure, rerun and recovery tested on purpose
checks.question: Does the test plan include deliberate failures: reruns, duplicate input, late data, schema changes, empty input and jobs killed mid-run?
checks.why: Every test assumed the happy path; in the first month the pipeline met a resent file, a late batch and a crash mid-write, and each one corrupted data.

evidence.looks_like: Negative test cases for each failure the design claims to handle, with expected outcomes.

checks.fail_fast: List every failure the architecture says it handles and check each has a test case.

checks.title: User acceptance scenarios designed late, without the users
checks.question: Were the user acceptance scenarios written during discovery, with the users who will test, and built around the questions they really ask and the figures they already know (last month's total for their region, a customer they can name)? When testing starts, will the testers know what to check, or will they click around and say it looks fine?
checks.why: The scenarios were written by the test team in the last week of the build, from the requirements alone. They checked that screens loaded, not that numbers were right, and the first month-end after go-live showed revenue a few per cent out in every region.

evidence.looks_like: A first set of acceptance scenarios agreed with named users by discovery sign-off, each one a real question with the expected figure from a trusted report for a known period, covering every user group and the tricky cases (returns, late data, reorganisations).

signals: The test strategy says "user acceptance testing" with no scenarios, or "scenarios to be defined".
Scenarios describe screens and clicks, not figures and expected values.
Scenarios were written by the project team with no named business contributor.
checks.contradiction: Compare the acceptance scenarios in the test strategy with the decisions and user groups in the requirements: a decision or user group with no scenario will be accepted without being tested.
checks.fail_fast: Ask two real users to write down three questions they will ask the new system and the answers they expect for last month; those are the first scenarios.

checks.title: Acceptance signed by the wrong people, or with no exit rule
checks.question: Will acceptance be signed by the people who will use the output, and is it agreed in advance what counts as accepted: which differences from the trusted figure are tolerable, and which open defects may go live? If testing ends with twenty open defects, is the go or no-go already decided?
checks.why: The project manager and the sponsor signed acceptance. The analysts who used the reports daily had found differences they could not explain, were not asked, and quietly went back to the old spreadsheets.

evidence.looks_like: Named acceptors from each user group, exit rules agreed before testing (tolerances for differences, severity of defects that may remain), and a dated sign-off record.

signals: Acceptance is signed only by the sponsor or the project team.
No exit criteria or tolerances are stated for user testing.
The sign-off template has no place to record open defects or conditions.
checks.contradiction: Compare the acceptors named in the test strategy with the user groups in the requirements: a user group with no acceptor has not accepted anything.
checks.fail_fast: Write the exit rule in three lines now and get the business owner and one real user to agree to it.

checks.title: Not every consumer and channel named
checks.question: Is every consumer of the output named, with the channel they use (dashboard, scheduled extract, file to a partner, application interface, machine learning model, AI assistant answering questions) and what each needs from it? Who will turn up at go-live asking where their feed is?
checks.why: The project built dashboards for the sales team. Two weeks before go-live the pricing team said their model read a nightly extract from the old system, which nobody had listed, and the cut-over was postponed.

evidence.looks_like: A consumer list: one row per consumer or channel with who they are, how they receive the data, what data and grain they need, how fresh, and any needs such as languages, accessibility or mobile use.

signals: Requirements describe only dashboards or reports, with no extracts, interfaces, models or assistants.
Downstream systems that read today's data are not listed.
Consumers are named as "the business" or "users" without groups.
checks.contradiction: Compare the consumer list in the requirements with the outputs drawn in the architecture: an output with no named consumer is unowned work, and a consumer with no output will be missed at go-live.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the source and current-report owners for the list of everyone who receives or queries today's data, and check each one against the requirements.

checks.title: Source-side changes not on the source team's plan
checks.question: For each change the project needs from a source (a new extract, a new field, change tracking switched on, a service account, a firewall rule), is it on the source team's or vendor's own plan, with a release date, a named contact and an escalation route? If the source team's next release slot is in four months, when will we find out?
checks.why: The project needed change tracking switched on in the source database. The source team agreed in a meeting, but their releases were quarterly and the next slot was full, so the build waited three months.

evidence.looks_like: A list of source-side changes, each with the item reference on the source team's own plan, the release date they committed to, a named contact and the person to escalate to.

signals: Source changes appear in the architecture but not as dependencies in the RAID log.
Dependencies on source teams have no date, or a date the source team has not confirmed.
No mention of the source team's release calendar or change freezes.
checks.contradiction: Compare the architecture's needs from each source with the RAID log's dependencies: a change the design needs that is not on the source team's plan is a date nobody has promised.
checks.fail_fast: Ask each source team for the reference number of the project's request on their own plan, and its release date.

checks.title: No agreement on how data is delivered
checks.question: Is there a written agreement with each source team or external supplier on what they deliver: by what time, in what format, how complete, how a late or broken delivery is reported and fixed, and in which support hours? When the file is late at 6 a.m., what does the agreement say happens?
checks.why: An external partner sent a daily file "in the morning". Some days it came at nine, some days at two, and the reports promised for eight o'clock were wrong half the week with nothing in writing to point to.

evidence.looks_like: A delivery agreement or contract schedule per source: delivery time, format, completeness check, notice of change, support hours, contact and escalation, and what happens when it is missed.

signals: Source delivery times written as "daily" or "overnight" with no clock time.
No support hours or contacts for external sources.
Freshness promised to users is tighter than anything a source has agreed to.
checks.contradiction: Compare the freshness promised to consumers with the delivery times agreed with sources: a report promised at 8 a.m. from a source that only promises "the morning" cannot keep its promise.
checks.fail_fast: Ask each source owner to state the latest time they will deliver and what they do when they cannot.

checks.title: Adoption never tracked
checks.question: After go-live, will anyone track who is using the new reports and data, compared with the old ones, and act when a user group does not move? Six months on, how will we know the people the project was built for are actually using it?
checks.why: The new dashboards went live on time and the project closed. Usage logs, read a year later, showed most managers had opened them once and gone back to spreadsheets exported from the old system.

evidence.looks_like: An adoption measure per user group (for example weekly active users of the new reports against use of the old ones), a target, a named person who reviews it monthly, and an action when a group lags.

signals: No adoption or usage measure in the plan or the benefits list.
The project closes on go-live with no review of usage afterwards.
Old reports keep running with no plan to compare their use with the new ones.
checks.contradiction: Compare the benefits in the business case with the measures planned after go-live: a benefit that depends on people using the new reports, with no usage measure, cannot be shown.
checks.fail_fast: Agree today which usage figure, read one month after go-live, would tell the sponsor adoption is failing.

checks.title: Benefits depend on business changes nobody owns
checks.question: For each promised benefit, is it written down what the business must change to get it (a process, a role, a meeting, a decision that now uses the new data), and who owns that change? If the data arrives perfectly and nothing improves, which business change did nobody make?
checks.why: The business case promised two days saved at each month-end. The data arrived early as designed, but the finance close process was never changed, so the team still waited for the old sign-off steps.

evidence.looks_like: A benefits map linking each benefit to the data the project delivers and to the business change it needs, with an owner and date for each business change.

signals: Benefits are described as outcomes of the data alone, with no business change named.
Process or role changes are mentioned as "the business will adapt" with no owner.
No business change tasks appear in any plan.
checks.contradiction: Compare the benefits in the business case with the scope: a benefit that needs a process change that is outside scope and owned by nobody will not arrive.
checks.fail_fast: For the biggest benefit, ask the business owner which process changes on day one and who will change it.

checks.title: Contingency hidden or missing
checks.question: Is contingency held as a separate, visible amount, sized to the riskiest assumptions, with a named person who can release it and a record of each use? When the data turns out worse than profiled, where will the money for fixing it come from?
checks.why: Every estimator padded their own numbers quietly. The padding was spent on gold-plating early on, and when the history load needed three extra weeks there was nothing left and no one could approve more.

evidence.looks_like: A contingency line linked to the top risks and assumptions, an owner who approves its use, and a log of drawdowns showing what each one paid for.

signals: No contingency in the budget, or a flat percentage with no link to risks.
Contingency described as "included in the estimates".
The risk log has high risks with costly mitigations that no budget line pays for.
checks.contradiction: Compare the risk log with the budget: high risks whose mitigation costs money, with no contingency to cover them, are unfunded risks.
checks.fail_fast: Price the mitigation of the top three risks and compare the total with the contingency held.

checks.title: Change requests with no cost
checks.question: Does every change request show what it adds in build cost, running cost and time, before anyone decides? If the project overspends, how much of it will be changes that were approved without a price?
checks.why: The business asked for the report to refresh hourly instead of daily. It was agreed in a demo as a small change, and it tripled the monthly compute bill and added two weeks of testing nobody had priced.

evidence.looks_like: A change log where each entry shows the build effort, the change to running cost, the effect on the date and the decider, with a running total of approved changes against contingency.

signals: Change records that state the request and the decision but not the cost.
Changes to freshness, history or volume approved without a running cost figure.
No running total of the cost of approved changes.
checks.contradiction: Compare the change log with the budget and forecast: changes approved since the baseline, with a forecast at completion that has not moved, means their cost was never added.
checks.fail_fast: Price the last three approved changes after the fact and add them to the forecast.

checks.title: Costs that sit in other teams' budgets
checks.question: Have the costs that land outside the project been found and agreed: the source team's work on a new extract, a vendor's fee for an interface or bulk export, extra environments, and running the old system during a parallel run? Who will refuse to pay for something the project cannot go live without?
checks.why: The source vendor charged for every change to the extract, and the source team had no budget for the work. The project waited two months while the two managers argued over who would pay.

evidence.looks_like: A list of costs the project causes in other teams or with vendors, with the amount, who pays, and the date each was agreed.

signals: Source changes, vendor interfaces or extra environments appear in the architecture with no cost or payer.
The old system's licence or support is due to end before the planned parallel run is over.
Phrases such as "the source team will provide" with no mention of their budget.
checks.contradiction: Compare the architecture's list of source changes and environments with the budget: each one that needs another team's work or a vendor's fee, with no agreed payer, is a stop waiting to happen.
checks.fail_fast: Ask each source owner and vendor whether the work the project needs from them is funded, and by whom.

checks.title: Technical words used with business people
checks.question: Are documents and reports written for the business in plain words, with technical terms explained or left out? When the business owner signs something, do they understand what it means for them?
checks.why: The design said history would be "type 1 for most dimensions". The business owner signed it, not realising it meant old addresses would be overwritten and last year's regional figures would change.

evidence.looks_like: Business-facing documents that state consequences in business terms ("last year's figures by region will change when a customer moves"), with a short glossary for unavoidable terms.

signals: Status or sign-off documents for the business use unexplained abbreviations and technical terms.
Decisions are described by their technical option, not by their effect on users.
No glossary in documents read by business stakeholders.
checks.contradiction: Compare a decision record with the business owner's own description of it (in notes or e-mail): if they describe a different consequence, the decision was not understood.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the business owner to explain the three biggest decisions back in their own words.

checks.title: Agreed in a meeting, lost afterwards
checks.question: Does every important meeting end with written actions and decisions, sent to the people affected and copied into the decision log or RAID log? A month from now, will anyone remember what was agreed today?
checks.why: The source owner agreed in a meeting to provide a daily extract by a set time. Nothing was written, the owner moved on, and the successor had never heard of it.

evidence.looks_like: Short meeting notes with actions (owner and date) and decisions, sent the same day, and decisions copied into the decision log.

signals: No meeting notes, or notes without actions and owners.
Actions in notes that never appear again in later notes or status reports.
Phrases such as "as discussed" referring to something with no written record.
checks.contradiction: Compare meeting notes with the decision log and RAID log: decisions and actions in the notes that are missing from the logs have been lost.
checks.fail_fast: After the next meeting, send three lines within an hour: decided, actions, open questions.

checks.title: Nobody knows who to call
checks.question: Is there a contact list for the project and the systems it depends on, including who to call when a source changes or a load fails, and how to escalate? If the pipeline fails at night in the first week of production, who is woken up and who do they call?
checks.why: A source was changed without notice and the load failed. Nobody knew who owned the source, so it took three days to find the right person while the reports stayed empty.

evidence.looks_like: A contact and escalation list for the team, each source, the platform, security and operations, with named people and a deputy for each.

signals: No contact or escalation list in the stakeholder map or runbook.
Source systems named in the architecture with no named owner.
Escalation described as "raise with management".
checks.contradiction: Compare the architecture's list of sources and systems with the contact list: a system with no contact is one that will fail silently.
checks.fail_fast: For each source, find the named owner and confirm they will tell the team before changing it.

checks.title: Assumptions never shared with the business
checks.question: Have the assumptions behind the estimate and plan been shown to the sponsor and the business owner, and do they know what changes if one of them breaks? If an assumption fails, will the business be surprised that the plan ever depended on it?
checks.why: The estimate assumed the business would provide testers for two weeks. The business never knew; when no testers came, user acceptance slipped by a month and the team was blamed.

evidence.looks_like: The key assumptions repeated in status reports and sign-off packs, with their current state (holding, at risk, broken).

signals: Status reports and steering packs do not mention assumptions.
Assumptions that require business action (testers, decisions, data) are not assigned to a business person.
checks.contradiction: Compare the estimate's assumptions with the status reports: assumptions in the estimate that never appear in any report have not been shared.
checks.fail_fast: Add a three-line "assumptions this plan depends on" box to the next status report.

checks.title: Steering packs that ask for nothing
checks.question: Does each steering pack open with the decisions and help the project needs from that meeting (a date, a budget release, a source team pushed, a definition settled), each with options and a deadline? After the next steering meeting, which blocker will still be blocked because we only reported progress?
checks.why: Steering packs ran to twenty slides of activity. The one line that mattered, that a source team had not started its extract change, sat on slide fourteen, and nobody in the room acted on it for three meetings.

evidence.looks_like: A first page listing the decisions and help needed, each with options, a recommendation and a deadline, and notes from the meeting recording what was decided.

signals: Steering packs contain progress and activity but no "decisions needed" section.
The same blocker appears in several packs with no request attached.
Steering notes record no decisions.
checks.contradiction: Compare open issues and decisions in the RAID log with the steering packs: an issue that needs steering action but never appears as a request in the pack is being reported, not escalated.
checks.fail_fast: Put "decisions we need from you today" as the first slide of the next steering pack.

checks.title: Running cost estimated from a real run
checks.question: What will the solution cost to run each month (compute, storage, transfer, licences), and is the figure based on a measured run rather than a guess?
checks.why: The business case assumed a few hundred a month; the first production bill was eleven thousand because the streaming jobs ran around the clock, and the project was paused for review.

evidence.looks_like: A monthly running cost estimate broken down by job and storage, derived from the thin slice or a test run scaled to production volume, agreed with the budget owner.

signals: Cost appears only as build effort, with no running cost.
checks.fail_fast: Read the actual cost of the thin slice's runs and multiply by production volume and schedule.

databricks.do: Read the thin slice's cost from system.billing.usage joined to system.billing.list_prices, by job.
databricks.verify: Compare the estimate with the first month of production usage from the same tables.
databricks.traps: List price is not your contract price; agree discounts with whoever holds the contract.

checks.title: No compute running when nothing needs it
checks.question: Is compute sized from real runs and does it stop when idle, rather than staying on or oversized "to be safe"?
checks.why: A job that needed ten minutes of compute held a large cluster for two hours each run because it waited on an upstream file, and nobody noticed for six months.

evidence.looks_like: Compute sizes justified by measured runs, automatic stop or job-scoped compute, waits on upstream data done outside paid compute, and a periodic review of utilisation.

checks.fail_fast: For the three most expensive jobs, compare the time compute was running against the time it was busy.

databricks.do: Use job compute or serverless for scheduled work instead of all-purpose clusters; set auto-termination; wait for upstream data with file-arrival or table-update triggers, not sleeping tasks.
databricks.verify: Compare job duration with compute uptime in system tables for the top jobs.
databricks.traps: A continuous Lakeflow pipeline or stream runs compute all day; use triggered mode when freshness allows.

checks.title: History depth asked for without a reason
checks.question: How many years of history does the business need, for which data, and what use requires that depth (year-on-year comparison, trend models, regulation)? If the history load doubles the estimate, will we know which part of it the business could live without?
checks.why: The business asked for "all history". Ten years were loaded at great cost, the oldest seven had different product codes nobody could map, and the only use was a two-year comparison.

evidence.looks_like: For each data area, the years of history needed, the use that needs them, whether old data must match today's definitions, and who will check the old numbers.

signals: History is requested as "all", "full" or "as much as possible".
A number of years is given with no reason.
Nobody is named to check that the loaded history matches what the business remembers.
checks.contradiction: Compare the history depth in the requirements with the history load in the estimate or plan: a different number of years, or none in the estimate, means the cost of history was never seen by the business.
checks.fail_fast: Ask: "Which report or decision needs data older than two years?" and price each extra year before agreeing.

checks.title: As it was, or as it is now, not decided
checks.question: When something changes over time (a customer moves region, a product changes category, a salesperson changes team), should past figures be reported under the old value or the new one, and for which reports? When last year's numbers move because of a reorganisation, will the business call it a bug?
checks.why: After a sales reorganisation, last year's revenue by region changed overnight because history was shown under the new regions. Finance needed it as it was originally reported, and the model had to be rebuilt.

evidence.looks_like: For each attribute that can change (region, category, team, status), whether reports should show the value at the time, the current value, or both, with a worked example the business has agreed.

signals: The requirements never say whether history is shown "as it was" or "as it is now".
Hierarchies or organisation structures are in scope with no mention of reorganisations.
The data model keeps history of changes for attributes the requirements never ask about, or the reverse.
checks.contradiction: Compare the requirements with the data model: an attribute the business wants "as it was" that the model stores only as the latest value has lost its history the day it changes.
checks.fail_fast: Take one real customer who changed region last year and ask the users which region last year's sales should appear under.

checks.title: Table retention matches time travel and recovery needs
checks.question: Is delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration (and log retention) set per table to match how far back the team needs time travel, RESTORE and stream recovery, balanced against storage cost and erasure rules?
checks.why: A bad release was found eight days later; VACUUM had already removed files older than the default seven days, so RESTORE to the good version was impossible.

evidence.looks_like: A retention setting per table class, justified by recovery needs and personal-data erasure deadlines.

checks.fail_fast: Run SHOW TBLPROPERTIES on key tables and compare retention with how long defects usually take to find.

checks.title: Auto Loader schema evolution mode chosen per source
checks.question: For each Auto Loader source, is the schema evolution mode (addNewColumns, rescue, failOnNewColumns, none) chosen deliberately, with the job set to restart after an intentional stop?
checks.why: With the default addNewColumns mode, a new source column stopped the stream as designed, but the job had no retries and the stream stayed down all night.

evidence.looks_like: The mode per source, where rescued data is monitored, and retries on the ingestion task.

checks.fail_fast: Drop a file with a new column in test and see whether the job recovers without a person.

checks.title: Pipeline expectations with the right action
checks.question: In Lakeflow pipelines, does each expectation use the right action (warn, drop row, fail update), and are dropped rows kept somewhere for reprocessing?
checks.why: Every rule was set to drop; thousands of rows a day were silently removed and only a count was logged.

evidence.looks_like: A rule list mapping each expectation to an action, plus a quarantine table for dropped rows.

checks.fail_fast: Count expectations by action in the pipeline code and check each drop has a quarantine.

checks.title: Promotion through bundles, run as service principals
checks.question: Are jobs, pipelines and dashboards deployed to each environment through Declarative Automation Bundles (formerly Asset Bundles) from CI, with production jobs running as a service principal?
checks.why: Production jobs were created by hand in the UI and ran as the developer; a later bundle deploy created duplicates and both copies wrote to the same tables.

evidence.looks_like: A bundle with dev, test and prod targets, run_as a service principal in prod, deployed only by CI.

checks.fail_fast: Deploy the thin slice to the test target with databricks bundle deploy from a CI pipeline.

checks.title: What a delete means downstream
checks.question: When a source deletes or soft-deletes a record, must it disappear, be flagged, or stay in each layer and report, and who decided?
checks.why: Engineers removed deleted customers from every table, but finance needed them kept for historic invoices, and last year's revenue dropped after a routine load.

evidence.looks_like: A rule per entity (remove, flag with a deleted date, or keep) agreed with the data owner, and how flagged rows are filtered in reports.

checks.fail_fast: Write the delete rule for the top three entities and get the data owner to sign them in one meeting.

checks.title: Deletes flow through derived tables
checks.question: When a source row is deleted, are the aggregates, summaries and extracts built from it recalculated too?
checks.why: The detail table dropped a deleted order, but the daily summary built from it was only ever appended to, so detail and summary disagreed and users stopped trusting both.

evidence.looks_like: Derived tables rebuilt for the affected periods when deletes arrive, and a test that checks detail and summary still agree after a delete.

checks.fail_fast: Delete one source row in test, run the full chain, and compare the summary total against the sum of the detail.

databricks.do: Enable Change Data Feed on silver so downstream jobs see deletes and rebuild affected aggregates.
databricks.verify: After a test delete, gold totals equal the sum of silver detail.

checks.title: Batch or streaming chosen for a reason
checks.question: Is the choice between batch, micro-batch and streaming justified by a stated freshness need and its cost, not by preference?
checks.why: The team built continuous streaming for a report read once a day; it cost eight times a nightly batch and was harder to support.

evidence.looks_like: A decision record linking the processing mode to a freshness number and a running cost comparison.

checks.fail_fast: Ask the consumer what decision they would take differently with data one minute old versus one hour old.

checks.title: One poison record does not stop the whole load
checks.question: Can a single malformed record (broken encoding, unparseable value, oversized field) stop the whole pipeline, and how is it isolated?
checks.why: One record with a malformed date crashed the stream parser on every retry; the pipeline was stuck for six hours while all later data waited behind it.

evidence.looks_like: Parsing that captures unreadable records into a side table with the raw content and the error, and a test with deliberately malformed input.

checks.fail_fast: Put one malformed record in the middle of a test input; the rest must load and the bad record must be kept somewhere readable.

databricks.do: Read files with a rescued data column (Auto Loader) or badRecordsPath, so malformed records are kept aside instead of failing the stream.
databricks.verify: Put a malformed record in a test file; the rest loads and the bad record is readable.

checks.title: Project fits the existing platform's standards
checks.question: Does the project follow the existing platform's environments, standards and shared frameworks, and are any exceptions agreed with the platform team?
checks.why: The project built its own ingestion code and its own environment layout; the platform team refused to support it at go-live and it had to be rebuilt.

evidence.looks_like: References to the platform standards and frameworks used, and a decision record for each deviation, signed by the platform team.

checks.fail_fast: Walk the platform team through the architecture for thirty minutes and list every point where they say "we don't do it that way".

checks.title: Guessed, not counted
checks.question: Was the estimate built by counting the things the project will deliver (sources, tables, rules, reports, interfaces) and multiplying by a rate, or was it a total someone felt was right? Could another person rebuild the number from the document?
checks.why: The estimate was "about three months" for the whole project. When it was finally counted there were forty tables and twelve reports, which at the team's real rate was nearer six months.

evidence.looks_like: A table of counted items by type and complexity, a rate per item, where the rate came from, and the total.

signals: The estimate is a total with no breakdown, or a breakdown by phase only.
No counts of sources, tables, rules or reports appear anywhere in the documents.
The rate per item is not stated or not explained.
checks.contradiction: Compare the estimate with the requirements or data model: if they list more sources, tables or reports than the estimate counted, the estimate is short.
checks.fail_fast: Count the items in the requirements yourself and divide the estimate by the count. If the effort per item looks implausibly small, it probably is.

checks.title: Escalation with no time limits
checks.question: Is there a written escalation path for blockers, saying how long a problem may stay at each level before it goes to the next, up to someone who can direct other teams? How many days can a blocked access request or a source team's refusal sit before the sponsor hears about it?
checks.why: A firewall change was blocked for seven weeks. The team kept chasing it politely, nobody had said when to escalate, and the sponsor learned of it when the date slipped.

evidence.looks_like: An escalation path with levels, named people and time limits (for example three working days at team level, a week at project manager level, then the steering group), and issues in the RAID log showing when they were escalated.

signals: Escalation described as "raise with management" with no names or times.
Issues in the RAID log open for weeks with no record of escalation.
Dependencies on other teams have slipped more than once with no escalation.
checks.contradiction: Compare the age of open issues in the RAID log with the escalation time limits: an issue older than its limit that was never escalated shows the path is not used.
checks.fail_fast: List every issue open longer than two weeks and escalate each one by Friday.

checks.title: Conditions from a gate never closed
checks.question: When a gate is passed "with conditions", is each condition written down with an owner and a date, and checked at the next gate? Which condition from discovery sign-off is still open, and does anyone remember it?
checks.why: Discovery was approved on condition that the source owner confirmed delete handling. Nobody tracked the condition, it was never confirmed, and deleted orders were still counted in production.

evidence.looks_like: Each gate condition recorded as an action in the RAID log with owner and date, and the next gate's pack showing the state of every earlier condition.

signals: Sign-off records say "approved with conditions" or "subject to" with no list of conditions.
Conditions from an earlier gate are not mentioned in later status reports or gate packs.
checks.contradiction: Compare the conditions in each sign-off record with the RAID log: a condition that never became a tracked action has been forgotten.
checks.fail_fast: Read the last sign-off record and list every condition with its owner and current state.

checks.title: Decision log and data dictionary not ready to hand over
checks.question: Will the support team receive a current decision log and data dictionary that explain why things are the way they are? When someone asks "why does this table work like this?" after the team has left, where is the answer?
checks.why: The support team "fixed" a rule that looked wrong. It had been agreed with finance a year before, but the decision was only in an old e-mail thread, and the change broke month-end reporting.

evidence.looks_like: A decision log and a data dictionary that match what is in production, reviewed as part of project closure.

signals: The decision log stops well before the end of build.
The data dictionary does not cover tables or rules added during build.
Handover lists code and access but not decisions or definitions.
checks.contradiction: Compare the data dictionary with the delivered data model or test results: rules in production that are not in the dictionary are unexplained.
checks.fail_fast: Ask someone outside the team to explain one business rule using only the handed-over documents.

checks.title: Benefits never measured
checks.question: Is there a plan to measure, after go-live, the benefits promised at the start, against the baseline taken before? A year after closure, can anyone prove the project was worth its cost?
checks.why: The business case promised hours saved each month. Nobody measured hours before or after, so the project could not show any return and the platform's next phase was refused.

evidence.looks_like: A benefits list with baseline values, the date and method of measurement after go-live, and an owner who will report the result.

signals: The business case or goals have no baseline figures.
No benefits review is planned after go-live.
The project closure report does not mention benefits.
checks.contradiction: Compare the goals in the discovery document with the closure or status reports: goals that are never reported on were never measured.
checks.fail_fast: Record today's value of each promised benefit, so there is something to compare against later.

checks.title: No exit criteria for early-life support
checks.question: Are there written criteria for ending the early weeks of close support after go-live (for example a number of clean runs, reconciled loads and no critical defects)? How will we know the system is ready to be left alone, rather than the team simply running out of time?
checks.why: The project team left after two weeks because the budget ended. Month-end processing, which had never run in production, failed the following week with nobody who knew the system.

evidence.looks_like: Written exit criteria for early-life support, covering at least one full business cycle, reconciled production loads and agreed defect levels.

signals: The plan ends at go-live, or has a fixed support period with no criteria.
Period-end or yearly processes are not mentioned in the early-life support period.
checks.contradiction: Compare the plan's early-life support period with the business calendar in the requirements: if the period ends before a month-end or other key cycle has run, the riskiest run happens unsupported.
checks.fail_fast: Ask: "Which business cycle has not yet run in production?" and keep support in place until it has.

checks.title: Source can bear the history extract
checks.question: Can the source system take the load of the history extract, and is the extract split into chunks that can each be retried?
checks.why: A single five-year query against the source database ran for nine hours, hit an undo limit and failed at ninety percent; it failed again the next night and slowed the source for its users.

evidence.looks_like: An extract split by date or key range, an agreed extract window with the source owner, and an estimate of run time per chunk from a real trial.

signals: The history load is one step with no chunking or restart point.
Source owners are not listed as reviewers of the extract approach.
checks.fail_fast: Time the extract of one realistic chunk against the real source in its normal busy window and multiply out; agree the result with the source owner.

databricks.do: For JDBC reads, set partitionColumn, lowerBound, upperBound and numPartitions and keep parallel connections within what the source owner agreed; or land extracts as files instead.
databricks.verify: Time one chunk against the source in its busy window.
databricks.traps: Too many partitions in a JDBC read opens that many connections at once against the source.

checks.title: Reloading or backfilling a past period
checks.question: Can a single past period (a day, a month) be reloaded or backfilled on demand without touching other periods or rebuilding everything?
checks.why: A source bug corrupted three days in March; the only way to fix them was a full rebuild that took the platform down for a weekend.

evidence.looks_like: Pipelines parameterised by period, writes that replace exactly that period, a runbook step for reloading a period, and a note on which downstream tables must also be rebuilt.

signals: The runbook has no reload or backfill procedure.
Jobs read "today" from the clock instead of taking the period as a parameter.
checks.fail_fast: In test, reload one day from three days ago with a parameter and check that only that day's rows and its downstream aggregates changed.

databricks.do: Pass the period as a job parameter and write with replaceWhere on the date column; keep a separate backfill job or bundle target for large reloads.
databricks.verify: Reload one past day in test; DESCRIBE HISTORY shows only that day's files were rewritten.
databricks.traps: A full refresh of a Lakeflow pipeline streaming table re-reads all source data and clears the table first; check source retention before pressing it.

checks.title: Time zones and business dates
checks.question: Which time zone does each source use, how are timestamps stored, and which time zone defines a business day?
checks.why: One source sent local time and another sent universal time; orders placed late in the evening fell into the next day and daily sales never matched the stores' own reports.

evidence.looks_like: The time zone of every source timestamp, a single storage convention, a defined business-day time zone, and a rule for daylight-saving changes.

signals: The data dictionary lists timestamps without a time zone.
checks.fail_fast: Pick ten real transactions near midnight and check that their business date matches what the source application shows.

databricks.do: Store timestamps as TIMESTAMP (universal time) and convert with from_utc_timestamp for the business-day time zone; set the session time zone deliberately rather than relying on defaults.
databricks.verify: Compare business dates of near-midnight rows with the source application.
databricks.traps: TIMESTAMP_NTZ has no time zone; mixing it with TIMESTAMP across sources shifts hours.

checks.title: No business glossary
checks.question: Is there one glossary of the business terms used in the requirements, reports and data model, each with a plain definition and an owner, kept where users and the team both look? When a new analyst asks what a term means, is there one place to point them?
checks.why: Three documents used "order", "booking" and "sale" for overlapping things. The developers treated them as the same, the users did not, and the confusion only came out in user testing.

evidence.looks_like: A glossary listing each business term, its plain definition, synonyms people use, the owner, and the fields or metrics it maps to.

signals: Requirements use several words for what may be the same thing (order, booking, sale).
Abbreviations and internal jargon appear with no definition.
The data dictionary describes columns but not business terms.
checks.contradiction: Compare the words used in the requirements with the names in the data model: a business term with no match in the model, or a model name no business person would recognise, shows the two speak different languages.
checks.fail_fast: List every noun in the top ten requirements and ask the business owner which are the same thing.

checks.title: Totals that cannot simply be added up
checks.question: For each metric that is a count of distinct things, a ratio, an average, a percentage or a balance at a point in time, has the business said how it rolls up across days, regions and products? When a user adds up the regional figures and gets a different total, will the definition explain why?
checks.why: Daily unique customers were summed to give a monthly figure, counting a customer who bought on ten days ten times. Margin percentages were averaged instead of recalculated. Both errors reached the board pack.

evidence.looks_like: Each metric marked as additive, partly additive (for example a stock balance that adds across stores but not across days) or not additive, with the rule for totals and a worked example.

signals: Ratios, averages, distinct counts or balances are defined with no rule for totals.
Requirements ask for the same metric "by day, week and month" with no word on how it rolls up.
Test cases check only the lowest level, not totals.
checks.contradiction: Compare the metric definitions with the report designs: a report that shows totals or subtotals for a metric with no roll-up rule will show a number nobody defined.
checks.fail_fast: For each ratio or distinct count, calculate the monthly total two ways on a real sample and show the business owner the difference.

checks.title: Every run leaves a record
checks.question: Does every run record what it read, what it wrote, row counts, duration and outcome, in a place that can be queried?
checks.why: A user reported a wrong figure from two weeks ago; with no run records nobody could say which load produced it or which input it came from.

evidence.looks_like: A run log or audit table with run id, inputs, outputs, counts, timings and status, kept for a stated period.

checks.fail_fast: Ask which source file produced a given row in yesterday's table, and see how long it takes to answer.
