databricks.do: Use system.lakeflow job and task run tables and DESCRIBE HISTORY for run records; add an audit table for business counts.
databricks.verify: Trace a row in gold to its job run and source file (_metadata.file_path captured in bronze).

checks.title: Production watched closely after go-live
checks.question: Were the first weeks in production watched closely (hypercare), with defects closed and operations running it alone before sign-off?
checks.why: The team moved to the next project on go-live day; a slow memory leak failed the job at month-end and nobody who understood it was available.

evidence.looks_like: A hypercare period with daily checks, a log of production issues and their fixes, and a handover point when operations run it alone.

checks.fail_fast: Put hypercare dates, people and exit criteria in the plan now.

checks.title: Retries for passing failures only
checks.question: Which failures are retried automatically (timeouts, throttling), how many times and with what wait, and which fail straight away (bad data, logic errors)?
checks.why: Every failure was retried five times; a bad-data error retried for three hours, burning compute and delaying the alert until the morning.

evidence.looks_like: A retry policy per job with limits and back-off, failures classified as transient or permanent, and an alert after the last retry.

checks.fail_fast: In test, cause one timeout and one data error; the first should retry and succeed, the second should fail fast and alert.

databricks.do: Set task retries and minimum retry interval, plus job and task timeouts and duration warnings.
databricks.traps: Retrying a non-idempotent task duplicates data; fix idempotency before adding retries.

checks.title: Two runs writing the same table at once
checks.question: What stops two runs of the same job, or two different jobs, writing to the same table at the same time?
checks.why: A manual rerun overlapped the scheduled run; both merged into the same table, one failed on a conflict, and the other left half-updated rows.

evidence.looks_like: One writer per table by design, a limit of one concurrent run per job, and a runbook rule for manual reruns.

checks.fail_fast: Start the same job twice in test and see what happens to the second run and the table.

databricks.do: Keep maximum concurrent runs at 1 (the default for new jobs) and use queueing for triggered jobs.
databricks.traps: Two different jobs writing one table can still conflict; Delta raises concurrent modification errors on overlapping files.

checks.title: Nobody approves changes to a definition
checks.question: After go-live, who may change a business definition or rule, how is the change requested, who approves it, and how are users told that past figures will move? When a manager asks the team to "just exclude" something, who has to say yes first?
checks.why: A regional director asked a developer to exclude one large customer from the margin report. The change went in quietly, the group margin moved, and finance found out when the board asked why.

evidence.looks_like: A definition change process: who can request, who approves (the definition's owner), how other users are consulted, how the change is versioned and dated, and how users are told.

signals: Definitions have owners but no process for changing them.
The support model handles technical changes but says nothing about changes to meaning.
Change requests to metrics go straight to developers.
checks.contradiction: Compare the definition owners in the data model with the support model's change process: if the support model lets the team change logic without the definition owner's approval, ownership exists only on paper.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the support lead: "If a director asks you tomorrow to change how revenue is counted, what do you do?"

checks.title: Mappings and hierarchies with no business maintainer
checks.question: Who in the business maintains the mappings and hierarchies the reports depend on (product to category, store to region, account to reporting line, cost centre to department), how do they change them, and how quickly? When a new product or store appears, who notices it is unmapped?
checks.why: New products launched every month. The mapping to categories lived in a spreadsheet the analyst who left had maintained, so new products fell into "unknown" and the category report drifted away from reality.

evidence.looks_like: A list of business-maintained mappings and hierarchies, each with a named maintainer, where it is edited, how often it changes, and what happens to records that are not yet mapped.

signals: Mappings or hierarchies are described as "reference data" with no owner.
Mappings are kept in personal spreadsheets or e-mailed files.
Nothing says what happens to a new code that is not in the mapping.
checks.contradiction: Compare the reference data in the data model with the support model: a mapping the reports depend on that no one in the support model maintains will go stale.
checks.fail_fast: Count how many codes in last month's source data are missing from today's mapping, and ask who would fix them.

checks.title: Volumes and growth stated
checks.question: What are the real volumes per source today (rows, size, files per day), and how much are they expected to grow over the next two to three years?
checks.why: The design was sized from a test sample of a million rows; production sent eight hundred million on month-end and the nightly window was blown on the first close.

evidence.looks_like: Measured volumes per source from real data, peak days (month-end, seasonal), and a growth assumption.

signals: Volumes are missing, or given as "large" or "medium" rather than numbers.
checks.fail_fast: Ask each source owner for the row count of their biggest table on their busiest day, and check one against a real extract.

checks.title: Skewed keys and very large joins
checks.question: Are there hot keys (one customer, one default value, nulls) or joins between two very large tables that will make some steps run far slower than the rest?
checks.why: Half of all rows carried a placeholder customer id; in the big join one worker processed that key for an hour while the others sat idle, and the job missed its window.

evidence.looks_like: Key distributions profiled for the large join keys, and a strategy for skewed keys and large joins (filtering defaults, splitting hot keys, pre-aggregating).

checks.fail_fast: Count rows per join key for the two largest joins and look at the top ten keys' share.

databricks.do: Rely on adaptive query execution for skewed joins, broadcast small tables, filter null and placeholder keys before joins, and salt only when AQE is not enough.
databricks.verify: In the Spark UI, compare the longest task against the median for the big join stage.

checks.title: Storage layout and file sizes kept healthy
checks.question: How are table layout (partitioning or clustering) and file sizes chosen and maintained, so frequent small writes do not slow reads over time?
checks.why: A streaming load wrote thousands of tiny files an hour; reads slowed every week until a simple query took ten minutes and cost ten times more.

evidence.looks_like: Layout chosen from the main filter and join columns, a scheduled compaction and cleanup job, and a metric for average file size.

checks.fail_fast: After a week of test loads, count files and average file size for the busiest table.

databricks.do: Use liquid clustering on the main filter or merge columns for new tables; let predictive optimization run OPTIMIZE and VACUUM on Unity Catalog managed tables.
databricks.verify: DESCRIBE DETAIL shows numFiles and sizeInBytes; DESCRIBE HISTORY shows OPTIMIZE runs.
databricks.traps: Predictive optimization covers managed tables only; external tables need scheduled OPTIMIZE and VACUUM. Check that clustering keys match the MERGE condition, or merges scan the whole table.

checks.title: Key-person risk
checks.question: Is there any part of the project that only one person understands or can do, and are the people the plan needs named and available when it needs them? If one person leaves next month, what stops?
checks.why: One developer understood the source system. When they moved to another project mid-build, the team lost six weeks rediscovering what they knew.

evidence.looks_like: Named people for each role with their availability, a second person for every critical area, and key-person risks on the RAID log.

signals: The same person's name appears as owner for most technical items.
Roles are listed as "to be hired" or "to be confirmed" for work in the next stage.
No mention of availability, leave or shared allocation.
checks.contradiction: Compare the plan with the stakeholder map or team list: a plan that needs a role the team list does not have, or a person allocated part-time who carries full-time tasks, will slip.
checks.fail_fast: Ask each team member which area they could not cover if a colleague were away for a month.

checks.title: The plan ignores the estimate's assumptions
checks.question: Does the plan use the same assumptions as the estimate (start of access, team size, environment availability, source readiness)? When the plan slips, will it be because it assumed something the estimate never did?
checks.why: The estimate assumed access in week three; the plan assumed week one. Nobody compared them, and the plan was two weeks behind before work started.

evidence.looks_like: A plan that lists the estimate's key assumptions and shows where each one sits on the timeline.

signals: The plan does not mention the estimate or its assumptions.
The plan's team size or start dates differ from the estimate's.
checks.contradiction: Compare the estimate's assumptions with the plan's dates and staffing: any mismatch is a slip already built in.
checks.fail_fast: Put the estimate's assumptions next to the first four weeks of the plan and look for disagreements.

checks.title: Open decisions with no owner, deadline or default
checks.question: Does every open decision have an owner, a date by which it is needed, and a default that applies if nobody decides? If the team is blocked next month, will it be waiting on a decision nobody owns?
checks.why: The choice between daily and hourly loads stayed open for ten weeks because nobody owned it. The team built for both, and later threw half away.

evidence.looks_like: An open-decisions list with the question, options, owner, the date needed, the default and the effect of deciding late.

signals: Open questions listed with no owner or due date.
Items the build depends on are marked "TBD" or "to be confirmed".
The same open question appears in several consecutive status reports.
checks.contradiction: Compare the open decisions with the plan: a task scheduled to start before the decision it depends on is due will either stall or be redone.
checks.fail_fast: Give every open decision an owner and a default today, and tell the owners the default applies on the due date.

checks.title: Discovery with no timebox
checks.question: Does discovery have a fixed length, a cost, and a list of exit criteria? If discovery runs for months or is squeezed into days, which risks will we carry into the build without having tested them?
checks.why: Discovery was squeezed into three days to "start building faster". The riskiest beliefs were never tested, and they surfaced one by one during the build.

evidence.looks_like: A discovery plan of a few weeks with weekly goals, its own estimate, named reviewers and written exit criteria.

signals: No discovery stage in the plan, or no end date for it.
Discovery has no estimate of its own.
No exit criteria for discovery sign-off.
checks.contradiction: Compare the discovery exit criteria with the discovery document: criteria that are not met but sign-off still happened show the timebox beat the evidence.
checks.fail_fast: Write the discovery exit criteria now and agree the end date with the sponsor.

checks.title: No parallel run period
checks.question: Where the new solution replaces an existing report or feed, is there a period when both run side by side, with a named person comparing them, a length that covers at least one month-end, and criteria for ending it? When the new number and the old number differ in week one, who decides which is right?
checks.why: The old report was switched off on go-live day. In the first month-end the new figures differed from what finance expected, there was nothing left to compare against, and trust in the new report never recovered.

evidence.looks_like: A parallel run on the plan with dates covering a month-end, a person who compares old and new, a tolerance, a decision owner for differences and written exit criteria.

signals: The old system or report is switched off on the go-live date.
Parallel running is mentioned with no length, owner or exit criteria.
The parallel run ends before the first month-end or quarter-end.
checks.contradiction: Compare the plan's parallel run dates with the business calendar: a parallel run that ends before the first month-end tests the easy days only.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the business owner which month-end they would want to see matched before switching off the old report.

checks.title: Team rolled off before the first month-end
checks.question: Does the plan and budget keep the people who built the solution available through early-life support, including the first month-end, quarter-end or other peak that the data will meet? When the first month-end load breaks, are the developers who wrote it still on the project?
checks.why: The developers moved to a new project the Monday after go-live. The first month-end load hit late corrections the tests never had, and support spent four days rebuilding knowledge the team could have given in an hour.

evidence.looks_like: Named people booked for early-life support, an end date after the first month-end or other peak, and the exit criteria for handing over fully to support.

signals: The plan and budget end on the go-live date.
Early-life support is mentioned but nobody is named or funded for it.
Team members are already booked on other projects from go-live.
checks.contradiction: Compare the plan's end date and staffing with the support model's early-life support period: a support period that outlasts the team's booking has nobody to do it.
checks.fail_fast: Check each developer's next booking date against the first month-end after go-live.

checks.title: Buffers not where data surprises cluster
checks.question: Does the plan hold explicit buffer time after the points where data projects usually find surprises: the first real extract, the first full load, the history load and the first reconciliation? Where in this plan would a two-week surprise from the data fit without moving go-live?
checks.why: Every task was planned back to back with no slack. The first full load showed that keys were not unique, and with nowhere to absorb the fix, every later date moved by the same three weeks.

evidence.looks_like: Named buffer tasks after the first real loads, the history load and reconciliation, sized to the risks in the RAID log, with a rule for who may use them.

signals: No buffer appears in the plan, or one buffer sits at the very end.
Tasks after the first full load and reconciliation are planned with no gap before go-live.
The RAID log has data risks with no time set aside for them.
checks.contradiction: Compare the data risks in the RAID log with the plan: a high data risk that hits in the middle of the plan, with no buffer after it, will move every later date.
checks.fail_fast: Ask where a two-week slip after the first full load would land, and whether the go-live date survives it.

checks.title: The business calendar ignored
checks.question: Has the plan been checked against the business and data calendar: month-end and year-end close, audit, peak trading, source system change freezes and the platform's own release windows? Which key date in our plan falls in a week when the business or a source team cannot help us?
checks.why: Go-live was set for the first week of January. Finance was closing the year, the source system was frozen for its own year-end, and the release had to wait until February.

evidence.looks_like: Business close periods, peak periods and change freezes marked on the plan, with no testing, cut-over or go-live inside them unless agreed.

signals: The plan shows no business calendar, freezes or close periods.
Go-live, cut-over or user acceptance falls in a month-end, year-end or known freeze.
checks.contradiction: Compare the plan's key dates with source teams' and the platform's change freezes: a release planned inside a freeze will not be allowed to happen.
checks.fail_fast: Ask finance, the source owners and the platform team for their freeze and close dates for the next year.

checks.title: Retention needs not stated by the business
checks.question: For each kind of data, how long does the business need to keep it, how long does law or policy require it to be kept, and when must it be deleted? When a user asks for seven-year trends and policy says delete after three, who decides?
checks.why: The business asked for ten years of customer history. Company policy required customer data to be deleted three years after the relationship ended, and the history load had to be cut back after it was done.

evidence.looks_like: A retention table per data kind: the business need, the legal or policy minimum and maximum, the agreed period, and who signed it, including what happens to aggregated figures after detail is deleted.

signals: Retention is not mentioned in the requirements, or is "to be agreed".
The history requested is longer than any retention period stated.
No one from records management, legal or compliance is named.
checks.contradiction: Compare the history depth requested in the requirements with the retention periods: history the business wants beyond the period policy allows must be resolved before it is loaded.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the records or compliance owner for the retention rule for the two most sensitive data kinds, and compare it with the history asked for.

checks.title: What must be proven to an auditor not stated
checks.question: Will auditors, regulators or internal control need to see how a reported figure was produced, reproduce a past figure exactly as it was reported, or see who changed what and when? Has the business written down those needs, so the design can meet them?
checks.why: A regulator asked the bank to reproduce a capital figure reported six months earlier. The data had been corrected since, nobody had kept what was reported, and the bank could not show where the number came from.

evidence.looks_like: A list of audit and control needs in business terms: which figures must be reproducible as reported and for how long, which changes need a record of who and when, and which reports need sign-off before release.

signals: Figures go to regulators, auditors or external parties but no audit need is stated.
The requirements never mention reproducing past figures, sign-off of published numbers, or change history.
Audit is mentioned only as access logging.
checks.contradiction: Compare the audit needs in the requirements with the restatement policy: if published figures may be restated but must also be reproducible as reported, the design has to keep both versions.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the finance or compliance owner: "Which number from this system could an auditor ask us to reproduce in a year's time?"

checks.title: Tolerances and who signs off differences
checks.question: What size of difference is acceptable for each measure, and who decides when a difference is explained well enough to go live?
checks.why: Test found a 0.3 percent gap; engineering called it rounding, finance called it a blocker, and go-live slipped two weeks while they argued.

evidence.looks_like: A tolerance per measure and a named person who accepts reconciliation results.

checks.fail_fast: Put the tolerance question on the next sign-off agenda and record a number for the top three measures.

checks.title: Branching and code review
checks.question: What is the branching approach, and must every change be reviewed by another person and pass automated checks before it merges?
checks.why: A developer pushed a join change straight to the main branch on a Friday; it removed a filter, and the weekend loads double-counted refunds.

evidence.looks_like: A short branching model, protected main branch, required reviewer, and automated tests and linting run on every pull request.

checks.fail_fast: Try to push directly to the main branch; it should be refused.

checks.title: Configuration per environment, not in code
checks.question: Are environment-specific values (paths, connection names, schedules, compute sizes) kept in configuration per environment rather than written into the code?
checks.why: A storage path to production was hard-coded in a shared module; tests in development read and then overwrote production data.

evidence.looks_like: A configuration file or variable set per environment, and code that reads all environment values from it.

checks.fail_fast: Search the code for production host names, paths and catalog names; each hit is a defect.

databricks.do: Use bundle variables and target overrides for catalog names, paths and compute sizes.
databricks.verify: Search the code for production catalog names outside the bundle configuration.

checks.title: The users are not the requesters
checks.question: Have the people who will use the output every day been asked what they need, or only the people who requested it? If nobody uses the system three months after go-live, will it be because it answered the requester's question and not the users'?
checks.why: A director requested a dashboard and approved the design. The analysts who were meant to use it needed row-level detail to act on, kept their old reports, and the dashboard went unused.

evidence.looks_like: Named users or user groups, how they will use the output, which decisions it supports, and evidence that some of them took part in workshops and will take part in user acceptance testing.

signals: Requirements name only a sponsor or requester, not users.
No user workshops, interviews or user personas are mentioned.
User acceptance testers are not named, or are the same person as the requester.
checks.contradiction: Compare the stakeholder map with the requirements sources: user groups on the map who are not listed as contributors to the requirements were never asked.
checks.fail_fast: Show a rough mock-up or a real sample of the output to three actual users and ask what decision they would make with it.

checks.title: Goals with no measure of success
checks.question: What business result is this project for, how will it be measured, and what is the measure today? A year after go-live, how will anyone know whether it was worth it?
checks.why: The goal was "better insight into customers". No measure was agreed, so at closure the project could not show any benefit, and the next request for funding was refused.

evidence.looks_like: Two or three goals, each with a measure, today's value (the baseline), a target, and where the data for measuring it will come from.

signals: Goals are written as activities ("build a data platform") rather than results.
No baseline figures are given for any goal.
Success measures need data the project does not collect.
checks.contradiction: Compare the goals in the discovery document with the scope: a goal whose measure depends on data or reports that are out of scope cannot be measured.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the sponsor to state the one number they hope will change, and check today whether that number can be produced.

checks.title: No trace from goal to requirement to test
checks.question: Can every requirement be traced back to a business goal or decision and forward to the data it needs, the thing that builds it and the test that proves it? When someone asks why a table exists, or whether a goal has been tested, can the team show it in minutes?
checks.why: A requirement for weekly churn by segment was dropped when the backlog was re-planned. Nothing linked it to the retention goal it served, so nobody noticed until the sponsor asked for the churn figure at closure.

evidence.looks_like: A simple trace table: goal, requirement, sources and fields, backlog item, test case, and status, kept up to date as items are added, changed or dropped.

signals: Requirements have no ids, or ids are not used in the backlog or test cases.
Goals and requirements live in separate documents with no link between them.
Test cases do not say which requirement they prove.
checks.contradiction: Compare the requirement ids in the requirements with those referenced in the test strategy: requirements with no test, and tests pointing at no requirement, show where the trace is broken.
checks.fail_fast: Pick the main goal and try to list, in ten minutes, every requirement and test that serves it.

checks.title: Requirements change without a version or a trail
checks.question: When a requirement, rule or definition changes, is the change versioned, dated, approved by its owner, and carried through to the data model, the backlog and the tests? If a tester tests against last month's version of a rule, will anyone know?
checks.why: The definition of an active customer changed twice in workshops. The data model held the first version, the tests the second, and the report the original, and user testing failed on all three.

evidence.looks_like: Requirements with a version and date, a change history per requirement or rule, the approver of each change, and a note of which designs and tests were updated.

signals: The requirements document has no version, date or change history.
Definitions or rules differ between the requirements, the data model and the test cases.
Changes are agreed in meetings or chat and not reflected in the requirements.
checks.contradiction: Compare the rule or definition text in the requirements with the same rule in the data model and test cases: any difference means a change reached some documents and not others.
checks.fail_fast: Take the three most-discussed definitions and check that the requirements, data model and tests say the same thing today.

checks.title: New joiners assumed productive on day one
checks.question: Does the plan allow for the time a new person needs before they are useful: laptop, accounts, access to sources and environments, security training and learning the domain? When a developer joins in week six, in which week will they first deliver?
checks.why: Two contractors joined to catch up the plan. Their access to the source data took four weeks to approve, so they were paid for a month of reading documents while the slip grew.

evidence.looks_like: An onboarding checklist with the lead time of each item, requests raised before the start date, and the plan showing reduced output for each new person's first weeks.

signals: People are added to the plan at full output from their first week.
No onboarding checklist or access lead times are written down.
Recovery plans rely on adding people late in the build.
checks.contradiction: Compare the plan's joining dates with the access request lead times in the RAID log: a person planned to deliver before their access can arrive will sit idle.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the most recent joiner how many days passed before they could query real data, and use that number.

checks.title: Users not ready on go-live day
checks.question: Are the users ready: told what is changing and when, trained on the new reports and what the numbers now mean, and pointed at where to ask for help, with the service desk briefed? On the first Monday, will users know why their numbers look different from last week?
checks.why: The new sales report used the agreed definition of revenue, which excluded returns. Nobody told the regional managers, who saw lower figures, assumed the report was broken, and kept using their old spreadsheets.

evidence.looks_like: A business readiness plan: user groups, messages and dates, training sessions with attendance, a short note on changed definitions and why numbers differ, and a briefed service desk.

signals: No training, user communication or service desk briefing is in the plan.
Definitions changed during the project but no user-facing explanation exists.
The only user communication is a go-live announcement.
checks.contradiction: Compare definitions that changed in the decision log or data model with the user communications: a changed definition users were never told about will be reported as a defect.
checks.fail_fast: Ask three future users what will change for them on go-live day, and note what they do not know.

checks.title: Old reports and feeds never switched off
checks.question: Is there a list of the old reports, extracts and spreadsheets the new solution replaces, each with an owner who agrees to switch it off and a date? A year after go-live, how many people will still be using the old numbers, and paying to run them?
checks.why: The old reports were left running "just in case". Two years later both sets were still in use, gave different answers in board meetings, and the cost of the old system was never saved.

evidence.looks_like: A switch-off list naming each old report or feed, its users, its owner, the switch-off date after the parallel run, and confirmation that it was done.

signals: The plan has no switch-off or decommissioning tasks.
Benefits depend on retiring an old system, but no retirement date exists.
Old reports are listed as "to be reviewed after go-live".
checks.contradiction: Compare the benefits in the business case with the switch-off list: savings that depend on retiring the old system, with no switch-off date, will not arrive.
checks.fail_fast: List every old report the new one replaces and ask each owner for a switch-off date.

checks.title: Clashes with other releases and platform changes
checks.question: Has the release been checked against other changes in the same window: source system upgrades, platform upgrades, other projects changing shared tables, network or identity changes? Which other team's release could break ours the same weekend?
checks.why: The project went live the same weekend the source system was upgraded. Two columns changed type, the first production loads failed, and nobody could tell which release had caused it.

evidence.looks_like: The release date checked against the change calendar for sources, the platform and shared data, with clashes recorded as dependencies or risks and agreed with the other teams.

signals: No mention of the change calendar or other releases in the deployment plan.
A shared platform or source upgrade is known but not on the RAID log.
Other projects write to tables this project reads, with no coordination recorded.
checks.contradiction: Compare the go-live date in the deployment plan with source and platform release dates in the RAID log or change calendar: two changes to the same system in one window will hide each other's faults.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the change board for every change planned to the sources and platform in the go-live week.

checks.title: The exceptions nobody mentioned
checks.question: Have the unusual cases been asked about and given rules: returns, cancellations, refunds, credit notes, intercompany sales, test and internal accounts, free items, split shipments, merged customers? Which exception will the users spot in the first week of testing?
checks.why: Nobody asked about staff purchases. They were twelve per cent of transactions at one site, were excluded from every report the business trusted, and were included in every number the new system produced.

evidence.looks_like: A list of exception types found in the data profile and in interviews, each with how often it occurs, and a rule for whether and how it counts in each metric.

signals: No requirement mentions returns, cancellations, internal accounts, test records or adjustments.
The data profile shows unusual record types or status codes that no requirement explains.
Rules cover only the standard case.
checks.contradiction: Compare the status codes and record types in the data profile with the business rules: every code with no rule will be treated by default, and the default is rarely what the business wants.
checks.fail_fast: List every distinct status or type code in the main source and ask the business owner what each one means and whether it counts.

checks.title: Which tables keep history, and for how long
checks.question: For each table, has the business decided whether to keep the history of changes or only the latest value, and for how long?
checks.why: Customer region was stored as latest only; when a sales team was reorganised, last year's sales by region were silently restated and the bonus calculation was disputed.

evidence.looks_like: A list of entities and attributes with "history kept" or "latest only", a retention period, and the business owner who agreed it.

signals: The data model has no statement about history for dimensions.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the main report owner "should last year's figures change when a customer moves region?" and record the answer as a decision.

checks.title: A business key that can change
checks.question: Can a source's business key ever change (renumbering, merges, re-registration), and how is the identity of the thing kept across that change?
checks.why: The source renumbered accounts during a migration; each renumbered account became a new customer, splitting its history and doubling the customer count.

evidence.looks_like: Surrogate keys owned by the platform, a mapping from old to new source keys, and the source owner's confirmation of whether keys can change.

checks.fail_fast: Ask each source owner directly whether keys are ever reused, merged or renumbered, and check a real extract for one key mapping to two names over time.

databricks.do: Generate surrogate keys with an IDENTITY column on the dimension; keep a source-key mapping table.
databricks.traps: IDENTITY values are unique but not consecutive, and declaring one limits concurrent writes to the table.

checks.title: Facts joined to the right version of history
checks.question: When facts are joined to a dimension that keeps history, are they matched to the version valid at the time of the fact, and is that the rule consumers expect?
checks.why: Facts were joined to the current customer row; reports that should show sales by the region at the time showed today's region instead, and nobody had written down which was wanted.

evidence.looks_like: For each report, whether it shows "as it was" or "as it is now", and joins that use the fact date within the validity range or the surrogate key captured at load.

checks.fail_fast: Take one customer who changed region last year and check a sales report shows each sale under the region the business expects.

checks.title: A new column appears at the source
checks.question: When a source adds a column, does the pipeline fail, drop it silently, or carry it through, and is that the agreed behaviour per layer?
checks.why: The source added a discount column; the raw layer dropped it silently, and when finance asked for it three months later the history could not be recovered.

evidence.looks_like: A schema policy per layer (for example: raw keeps everything including unknown columns, cleaned layers change only through a reviewed change), and an alert when a new column appears.

signals: The architecture does not mention schema changes at all.
checks.fail_fast: Add a column to a test source file or table and run the pipeline; see what each layer does and whether anyone is told.

databricks.do: Choose an Auto Loader schemaEvolutionMode per source: addNewColumns (default when no schema is given; stream stops once, then continues with the new column), rescue (new columns go to _rescued_data), failOnNewColumns, or none. In silver, use MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION only where agreed.
databricks.verify: Drop a test file with an extra column and watch what the stream and the target do.
databricks.traps: With addNewColumns the stream fails on purpose and must be restarted; make sure the job has retries, or it stays down overnight.

checks.title: Source owners warn before they change
checks.question: Is there an agreement (a data contract or a change notice) that source owners tell the data team before changing structure or meaning?
checks.why: The source team released a new version on a Friday with restructured tables; nobody told the data team and the weekend loads failed, missing a regulatory deadline.

evidence.looks_like: A written agreement or contract per source naming the schema, the notice period for changes, and a contact; source release calendars known to the team.

signals: Source owners are not in the stakeholder map.
checks.fail_fast: Ask each source owner when their next release is and whether it changes anything the project reads.

checks.title: "Phase 2" used as a hiding place
checks.question: Is everything labelled "phase 2" or "later" actually planned, funded and owned, and does the business know that phase 2 may never happen? If phase 2 is cancelled, will the first phase still be useful on its own?
checks.why: Hard items such as history and data quality were moved to phase 2 to make the first phase look affordable. Phase 2 was never funded, and phase 1 was unusable without them.

evidence.looks_like: A "later" list in which each item states whether phase 1 depends on it, an owner, and whether funding exists, plus a statement that phase 1 is usable without them.

signals: Many items marked "phase 2", "future phase" or "later" with no dates or owners.
Phase 2 has no estimate or budget.
Items that the main goal depends on are listed under phase 2.
checks.contradiction: Compare the goals or success measures with the phase-2 list: a goal that can only be met by phase-2 items means phase 1 alone does not deliver the value promised.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the sponsor: "If there is no phase 2, would you still pay for phase 1 as written?"

checks.title: MVP 1 is too big
checks.question: Is the first MVP the smallest slice that gives real value and proves the hardest parts work end to end? If the first release slips by months, will it be because it tried to do everything at once?
checks.why: MVP 1 contained eight sources and every report. Nothing reached production for nine months, so no real feedback arrived until it was too late to change direction.

evidence.looks_like: An MVP 1 that can reach production within a few months, chosen for value and for testing the riskiest beliefs, with later MVPs listed in order of dependency and value.

signals: MVP 1 contains most or all of the in-scope items.
The first production release date is more than about three months after build starts.
The reason for the MVP order is not written down.
checks.contradiction: Compare the plan's MVP 1 with the estimate: if MVP 1 holds most of the estimated effort, it is the whole project with a different label.
checks.fail_fast: Ask what could be removed from MVP 1 while it still gives one group of users a real answer.

checks.title: Scope not signed by the business owner
checks.question: Has the person who will judge success signed the in, out and later lists, and is that signature recorded with a date? If scope is disputed later, whose signature ends the argument?
checks.why: The scope was agreed with a delegate. The real business owner saw it for the first time at user acceptance and rejected half of the out-of-scope list.

evidence.looks_like: A dated sign-off record naming the business owner, the version of the scope signed, and any conditions.

signals: The scope document has no approver, approval date or version.
Approval is recorded as "agreed in meeting" without a name.
The approver is not the business owner named in the stakeholder map.
checks.contradiction: Compare the scope sign-off with the stakeholder map: if the person who signed is not the one the map names as the decision owner, the sign-off may not hold.
checks.fail_fast: Send the out-of-scope list to the business owner today and ask for a written yes.

checks.title: Consumers can tell whether data is complete
checks.question: Can a consumer see when the data was last refreshed and whether today's load is complete, before they rely on it?
checks.why: The load failed overnight but the dashboard looked normal; the sales director presented yesterday's numbers as today's to the board.

evidence.looks_like: A visible "data as of" time on reports, a completeness flag or status table, and a way to warn consumers when a load is late.

checks.fail_fast: Stop the load in test and look at the report as a user would; can you tell it is stale?

databricks.do: Publish a status table or use table health in Catalog Explorer from data quality monitoring; show last refresh time on AI/BI dashboards.

checks.title: Changes to what consumers use are announced
checks.question: How are breaking changes to published tables or interfaces versioned and announced, so consumers have time to adapt?
checks.why: A column was renamed for consistency in a minor release; three reports and a partner extract broke the next morning.

evidence.looks_like: A rule separating published interfaces from internal tables, a versioning or deprecation approach with a notice period, and a list of who to tell.

checks.fail_fast: Find out how the team would learn which consumers use a given column today.

checks.title: Consumer queries fast enough under real load
checks.question: Will reports, interfaces and extracts respond fast enough when the expected number of users or calls hit them at the same time?
checks.why: The dashboard was quick in testing with one user; on Monday morning two hundred managers opened it at once and it took two minutes per page.

evidence.looks_like: Expected concurrent users or calls and response targets, the serving design (aggregates, caching, sizing), and a concurrency test result.

checks.fail_fast: Run the slowest report query twenty times at once against realistic data and time it.

databricks.do: Serve reports from a SQL warehouse sized and scaled for concurrency; pre-aggregate heavy gold tables or use materialized views.
databricks.verify: Run concurrent queries and read the warehouse's query history for queueing time.

checks.title: Conflicts left unsaid
checks.question: Where stakeholders want different things (speed against cost, one department's definition against another's), is the conflict written down with options and taken to the decision owner? Which disagreement are we avoiding that will surface at sign-off?
checks.why: Finance wanted monthly figures to match the ledger; sales wanted daily figures fast. Nobody named the conflict, the design pleased neither, and both refused to sign.

evidence.looks_like: Conflicts recorded as issues or open decisions, with each side's need, options, a recommendation and a deadline.

signals: Requirements from different groups that contradict each other with no note of the conflict.
Meeting notes saying a topic was "taken offline" repeatedly.
No issues or open decisions involve more than one stakeholder group.
checks.contradiction: Compare requirements from two different stakeholder groups: requirements that cannot both be met, with no decision recorded, are a hidden conflict.
checks.fail_fast: Put the two conflicting needs on one page with options and send it to the decision owner this week.

checks.title: Sign-off without reading
checks.question: Did the people signing get the document in time to read it, and are their findings answered in writing? Is anyone signing something they have not read or do not agree with?
checks.why: Reviewers saw the discovery document for the first time in the sign-off meeting and approved it to keep things moving. Their real objections arrived in the build, where they cost ten times more.

evidence.looks_like: The document sent to reviewers several days before sign-off, a list of findings with written answers, and a sign-off record naming who approved what.

signals: No review comments or findings are recorded before sign-off.
The document was distributed on the same day as the sign-off meeting.
Sign-off is recorded for a group ("the steering committee") with no individual names.
checks.contradiction: Compare the sign-off record with later status reports or change requests: early objections to items that were signed suggest the signers had not read them.
checks.fail_fast: Ask each signer, before the meeting, for their single biggest concern in writing.

checks.title: Sponsor or owner changes and nobody re-confirms
checks.question: When the sponsor, business owner or a key data owner changes during the project, is the new person taken through the scope, definitions, decisions, budget and dates, and asked to confirm them in writing? If a reorganisation replaces our sponsor next month, which agreed decision is the new one most likely to reopen?
checks.why: The business owner moved roles after discovery sign-off. Her successor had never seen the definitions, did not accept the agreed treatment of returns, and two months of modelling were redone.

evidence.looks_like: A record of each change in key stakeholders, the briefing given to the new person, and their written confirmation (or the decisions they reopened, handled as change requests).

signals: Names in recent status reports or meeting notes differ from those on the stakeholder map or sign-off record.
A new sponsor or owner appears with no record of a handover briefing.
Signed decisions are being questioned again in meeting notes after a change of people.
checks.contradiction: Compare the signatories on the discovery sign-off with the people now named as sponsor and owners: a decider who did not sign has not yet agreed.
checks.fail_fast: Check whether everyone who signed discovery still holds the same role, and brief anyone new this week.

checks.title: Automated tests run on every change
checks.question: Do automated tests (code and data) run on every change in the release pipeline, and does a failure stop the release?
checks.why: A small refactor changed a join; the tests existed but were run by hand and nobody ran them, so the regression reached production.

evidence.looks_like: Tests wired into the pull request and deployment pipeline as required gates, with coverage of the transformations that carry business rules.

checks.fail_fast: Break one business rule deliberately on a branch; the pipeline must fail before merge.

databricks.do: Run unit tests with pytest locally or with Databricks Connect, and data tests in a CI job deployed by the bundle to a test target.

checks.title: No data or environment for user testing
checks.question: What data will business testers use (real enough for them to recognise their numbers, covering a period they know), in which environment, with what access, and is personal data in it allowed? If testers cannot log in on the first day, or see numbers they cannot judge, how many testing days are lost?
checks.why: User testing used invented data so that no personal data left production. The testers could not tell whether any figure was right, signed off out of politeness, and the first real month showed the errors.

evidence.looks_like: A statement of which period and data the testers will use, how it is made safe if it holds personal data, which environment they use, and that their access was requested and tested before testing starts.

signals: The test strategy says user testing will use "test data" or "sample data" with no period named.
Business testers' access to the test environment is not in the plan.
Nothing says whether personal data may be used in user testing.
checks.contradiction: Compare the user testing approach in the test strategy with the platform environments: user testing that needs production-like data in an environment that is not allowed to hold it cannot happen as planned.
checks.fail_fast: Ask one business tester to log in to the test environment this week and find last month's figure for their own area.

checks.title: Self-service expectations not stated
checks.question: Does the business expect users to build their own reports and answer their own questions, and if so, which users, with what skills, on which data, with what training and support? If users say at go-live "we thought we could build our own", will that be in scope?
checks.why: The sponsor expected analysts to explore the data freely. The team built fixed reports only, with no documented model for users to build on, and the analysts went back to exporting to spreadsheets.

evidence.looks_like: A clear statement of who will only read reports and who will build their own, what data the builders may use, what training and documentation they will get, and who supports them.

signals: Words such as "self-service", "explore" or "ad hoc" appear with no named users or scope.
No training, documentation or support for business users is in the plan.
The out-of-scope list says nothing about self-service.
checks.contradiction: Compare the self-service promises in the discovery document with the plan and handover: self-service promised but no user documentation, training or support planned will not happen.
checks.fail_fast: Ask the sponsor to name three people who will build their own reports, and ask those three what they plan to build.

checks.title: Licences and contract terms for getting the data
checks.question: Do the contracts with source system vendors allow the project to extract the data in the way and volume the design needs, and are the licences for every tool and user covered? Which clause will we discover the week before go-live?
checks.why: The design pulled history through the vendor's interface. The contract capped calls per day and charged for bulk export, which nobody had read, so the history load needed a new commercial agreement.

evidence.looks_like: A note per vendor source and tool of the contract terms checked (extract rights, call limits, export fees, data use), the licence count needed against the count owned, and who checked it.

signals: Vendor-hosted sources in the architecture with no mention of contract terms or limits.
Licences for report users or tools are not mentioned in the budget.
The number of users planned is larger than the licences held, or the count is unknown.
checks.contradiction: Compare the history load and refresh approach in the architecture with the vendor's stated limits: a design that needs more calls or bulk export than the contract allows will be stopped.
checks.fail_fast: Send the vendor the planned extract approach and volumes and ask them to confirm it is allowed at no extra cost.

checks.title: Supplier work with no acceptance or handover terms
checks.question: If an outside supplier builds part of the solution, does their contract say what "done" means (tested, reconciled, documented), how it is accepted, who fixes defects after go-live and for how long, and what knowledge they must hand over? When the supplier's contract ends at go-live, who fixes the first broken load?
checks.why: The supplier was paid on delivery of the pipelines. Their contract ended at go-live, the first month-end load failed, and the internal team had no documentation and no right to ask the supplier back.

evidence.looks_like: A statement of work with acceptance criteria tied to tests and reconciliation, a warranty period that covers the first month-end, and handover deliverables with dates.

signals: Supplier deliverables are described as code or pipelines, with no tests or documents.
The supplier's contract ends on or before the go-live date.
No warranty or defect-fix period is mentioned.
checks.contradiction: Compare the supplier's end date with the plan's early-life support period: a supplier who leaves before support ends leaves the defects behind.
checks.fail_fast: Read the supplier's acceptance and end-date clauses against the go-live and month-end dates this week.

checks.title: No regular rhythm for updates
checks.question: Is there an agreed rhythm for telling stakeholders what was learned, what changed, and what is needed from them? Which stakeholder will say they heard nothing for a month?
checks.why: Updates went out only when there was good news. Stakeholders filled the silence with rumours and the sponsor started asking for daily reports, which took the team's time away from the work.

evidence.looks_like: A communication plan stating who gets what and how often, and status reports that follow it.

signals: No communication plan.
Gaps of several weeks between status reports.
Status reports go to the sponsor only.
checks.contradiction: Compare the communication plan with the actual status reports: a planned weekly update that appears monthly is a rhythm that broke.
checks.fail_fast: Send a three-line update this Friday: what we learned, what changed, what we need from you.

checks.title: Cost can be traced to a team and a job
checks.question: Can the running cost be broken down by project, team, environment and job (by tags or separate accounts), so overruns can be traced?
checks.why: The platform bill doubled in one month and nobody could say which project caused it, so every team was asked to cut costs instead of the one that needed to.

evidence.looks_like: A mandatory tagging standard (project, owner, environment), enforced on compute and storage, and a cost report by tag.

checks.fail_fast: Pull last week's cost broken down by project tag; check how much is untagged.

checks.title: Lessons captured only at the end
checks.question: Are lessons gathered at each gate and after each MVP, with an action that changes how the next stage is run? If the same data surprise hits MVP 2 that hit MVP 1, will anyone have written down how to avoid it?
checks.why: The first MVP lost three weeks to late source access. The lessons review was held at project closure, so MVP 2 and MVP 3 lost the same three weeks for the same reason.

evidence.looks_like: A short lessons list after each gate and MVP: what happened, what we will do differently, the owner of that change, and evidence in the next stage's plan that it was done.

signals: The only lessons review in the plan is at project closure.
The same kind of issue appears in the RAID log for more than one MVP.
Lessons are listed with no action or owner.
checks.contradiction: Compare the lessons from one stage with the plan for the next: a lesson with no matching change in the next plan has not been learned.
checks.fail_fast: Spend fifteen minutes at the next retrospective on one question: what will we change for the next MVP?

checks.title: Success not defined for each stakeholder
checks.question: Has each key stakeholder been asked what success looks like for them and what has gone wrong for them before? If a stakeholder calls the project a failure, will we know in advance what they were measuring?
checks.why: The sponsor wanted lower cost, operations wanted fewer night calls, and users wanted faster reports. The project delivered only faster reports and was seen as a failure by two out of three.

evidence.looks_like: For each key stakeholder, one line on what success means to them and a note of past problems they raised.

signals: The stakeholder map lists names and roles but not interests or success measures.
No record of initial interviews with stakeholders outside the business owner.
checks.contradiction: Compare each stakeholder's success measure with the scope: a measure that nothing in scope can move is a disappointment already planned.
checks.fail_fast: Ask each stakeholder one question this week: "What would make you say this project worked?"
